- ch. 7 "Welcome to the Neighborhood" *(no index entry yet)* — Editor Holly Mohr's introduction recounts receiving Plato's Republic and Apology for a summer program and realizing she had been philosophizing since childhood, and that Fred Rogers would not have been surprised: wonder is what children do best and what philosophy is. She argues Rogers takes children seriously as full persons, shows through his visits to workers, farmers, and children with disabilities that wonder is available in every life, and that meaning is made together in the Neighborhood, in community rather than solitude.
- ch. 8 "Thanks" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "I Did You Know It’s All Right to Wonder" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "1. The Wonderful Feeling of Being Alive" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Jacob Graham reads the show's behind-the-scenes honesty (episode 1530's studio tour, Rogers showing the puppets dead in his bag) through Plato's Theaetetus claim that philosophy begins in the feeling of wonder and its call for the philosopher's leisurely slowness (skole), which Rogers built into television through silence and a low pace. Drawing also on Aristotle's Metaphysics, he argues wonder at the sheer being of ordinary things ends in reverent silence before each person's unrepeatable uniqueness, which Rogers treats as axiomatic: 'I like us just the way we are.'
- ch. 11 "2. Mesmeric Mister Rogers" **·** Sigmund Freud, Walter Benjamin — The Unconscious — Marlene Clark argues Fred Rogers was a mesmerist in the lineage of Franz Mesmer's animal magnetism, a hypnotic appeal that survived mesmerism's debunking by passing into Freud and Breuer's psychoanalytic transference and into the primitive, unconscious sex appeal of screen idols like Brad Pitt. She details episode 1588, where Rogers defuses bathtub-drain fears with 'You Can Never Go Down the Drain' and scuba-suited Neighbor Aber frightens Henrietta Pussycat, and the 1969 Senate hearing where reciting 'What Do You Do with the Mad That You Feel?' visibly entranced Senator Pastore into awarding PBS 20 million dollars.
- ch. 12 "3. Wonder and Philosophy as a Way Home" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, Pythagoras — Platonic Love (the ladder of love); Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know); Pythagorean Harmony of the Spheres — Nathan and Leilani Mueller argue the theme song's 'neighborly day in this beautywood' makes beauty a transcendental leading to wisdom, as in Plato's Symposium ascent to loving the beautiful itself and Aquinas's convertibility of truth, goodness, and beauty. Reading Rogers's questioning of batteries and boxes (episode 1655) through the Meno's genuine curiosity and Pierre Hadot's account of philosophy as a way of life, they tour the show's three philosophical spaces: the domestic living room, the community visit (blind saxophonist Eric Kloss), and Make-Believe as thought experiment.
- ch. 13 "4. The Gently Socratic Inquiry of Fred Rogers" **·** Socrates, Plato — Socratic Method (elenchus); Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — Ben Lukey and Steve Bein, veterans of p4c Hawai'i, argue Rogers ran a 'gently Socratic' community of inquiry on television: unlike Socrates the public gadfly who made asses of interlocutors, Rogers created intellectual safety, treating Daniel Striped Tiger's 'What does assassination mean?' (after MLK's murder) and the Officer Clemmons kiddie-pool scene as philosophy with children. Using Dr. Tom Jackson's Good Thinker's Toolkit to show children are philosophers, they defend 'little p philosophy' as activity over 'Big P Philosophy' as content, casting Rogers and Socrates as midwives rather than lecturers.
- ch. 14 "II What Do You Do with the Mad that You Feel" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "5. Another Day in the Neighborhood" **·** Plato, Immanuel Kant, Martin Heidegger — Tripartite Soul; Autonomy of the Will; Authenticity; The They-Self (das Man) — Sydney Ball and Eric Mohr interleave a college student's Tuesday with her six-year-old self watching the show: Plato's Republic (439c) on the rational part overruling the appetitive frames procrastination and lost youthful energy, Kant's autonomy frames doing what you should without being told, and Heidegger's 'They' frames her supermarket jealousy, dissolved by complimenting a stranger's shoes just as Henrietta Pussycat overcame jealousy of Grandpere's fancy granddaughter Collette (episodes 1176-1180). The lesson, learned from Mister Rogers's words about stopping, is authenticity: 'I like you just the way you are.'
- ch. 16 "6. Peace through Emotional Development" *(no index entry yet)* — Nathaniel McDonald and Frank Scalambrino read the show as a Montessori 'prepared environment': like Montessori's planes of development, Rogers designed every consistent transition, song, and set detail (shoe swap, Trolley, feeding fish) for children's developmental needs, aiming at self-regulation so the child can manage 'the mad that you feel.' Grounding 'It's You I Like' in Carl Rogers's unconditional positive regard and Montessori's syllogism that education is the work of peace, they rebut the entitlement critique as a correlation-causation fallacy and a misinterpretation of freedom-with-responsibility.
- ch. 17 "7. Feelings, Mentionable and Manageable" **·** Phenomenology — Jonathan Heaps takes Rogers's Senate line that 'feelings are mentionable and manageable' and supplies its philosophical engine in Eugene Gendlin's theory of experiencing and symbolization: there is the anger and there is feeling-the-anger, and attending to that felt quality, as Henrietta does when X the Owl bosses her during fruit salad (episode 1508), lets a symbol like 'mad' or the image of 'a big scary animal on a chain' name it. Because symbolizing changes the felt meaning of the experience, mentioning feelings genuinely manages them, which is why the 'What Do You Do with the Mad That You Feel?' song works.
- ch. 18 "III By Pretending You Can Be Most Anything You Can Think About" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "8. The Virtues of Art" **·** John Dewey — Experience and Education — David Boersema, opening with Mister Miyagi's chores in The Karate Kid, argues Rogers used the arts for four virtues: affective meaning (King Friday is 'pigheaded' where another is 'firm'), art as both product and process (pottery lessons and Eric Hill's studio, episodes 1644-1645), art as communication and community (Robert Troll's portrait of Lady Elaine softening her; sharing children's Trolley drawings as love), and art as transformation, from Aristophanes' Lysistrata to Dewey's dictum that art is not a thing but an experience, with Rogers's tree and fish songs as gentle social activism.
- ch. 20 "9. Fred’s Felt Friends" *(no index entry yet)* — Daniel Leonard explains children's devotion to the Make-Believe puppets through Donald Winnicott's transitional objects: soft puppets work like blankies bridging inner and outer reality, as when Rogers answered a toddler's letter that Make-Believe has no time 'like the timelessness of love.' Adding Bandura's observational learning and Horton and Wohl's parasocial interaction, he argues the show's structure (attention, retention, initiation, motivation) makes Lady Aberlin's 'You're no mistake' duet with Daniel Striped Tiger a safe mediated space where children rehearse being persons.
- ch. 21 "10. Play in the Real World" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce, William James, John Dewey — Pragmatism; Experience and Education — Elizabeth Cooke reads Rogers's double movement, demystifying reality (the studio reveal in episode 1530, the otoscope that cannot see into minds) while insisting 'anything is possible in make-believe,' as pragmatist epistemology: rejecting Plato's two worlds and Cartesian doubt, Rogers agrees with Peirce's open-ended 'musement,' Santayana's play as a 'holiday' revealing truer selves, and James's malleable world that our creativity 'adds to.' Pretend, as when Daniel wonders if he is a mistake or children take others' perspectives in competition episodes, is how children actively learn what is most real, with George Herbert Mead explaining how perspective-taking builds the self.
- ch. 22 "11. Mister Rogers’s Pseudonyms" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — Hoon Lee argues Rogers never appears in the Neighborhood of Make-Believe because the puppets are his pseudonyms, reproducing Kierkegaard and Hamann's indirect communication: the child works through fear and anger at a safe distance, as when Daniel Tiger asks Lady Aberlin what 'assassination' means, before the Trolley returns to Rogers's direct speech. He extends the point to the show's contemplative aesthetics (silence, slow cake-piping), the coded '143' for 'I love you,' and the 1969 kiddie-pool scene with Officer Clemmons as indirect communication against segregation.
- ch. 23 "12. Puppets Are People Too" **·** Anthropocentrism — Sara Lindey and Jason King argue that making puppets persons, from King Friday's 'Life is good. Being a person is good. Breathing air is good' to interspecies cousins and adoptions (Ana the puppet adopting costumed Bob Dog), resists the Anthropocene's human exceptionalism and its exploitation of a world of mere resources. Via Timothy Morton's solidarity with nonhuman people and Donna Haraway's cyborg blurring of human, animal, and machine, they read the puppeteer as an emotionally enhanced cyborg and the 1990 trash-cataclysm week, solved by recycling goats, as Rogers's ecological family of neighbors.
- ch. 24 "13. Won’t You Be My Posthuman Neighbor" **·** Anthropocentrism — Fernando Pagnoni Berns reads the show as posthumanist: the toy-model opening credits leave it unclear whether Rogers himself is a toy, Trolley refuses orange juice yet speaks (an object with a will), Lady Aberlin uses a bass as a dance partner, and Audrey Duck's 'You're as real as you want to be' collapses human, animal, and hand puppet. Invoking Bruno Latour's quasi-human 'non-humans' that channel human desires, he argues the Neighborhood dissolves the humanist hierarchy that enthrones the white Western male over women, animals, objects, and plants.
- ch. 25 "IV You Are My Friend, You Are Special to Me" *(front)*
- ch. 26 "14. A Party to Celebrate the Personal" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on the Soul — Eric Mohr reads the 'Everybody's Special' week, Prince Tuesday shedding his royal cape because 'It's what's inside you that makes you special,' the plate factory that discards irregular plates, and King Friday's sameness mask-edict undone by Lady Elaine, as Max Scheler's personalism: persons are unique, unrepeatable 'individual value-essences' whose value only love discloses, which is why Corney's birthday party matters. Against the Aristotelian view that the soul is one universal form and our bodies merely individuate us, Scheler and Rogers hold the inner self is where difference deepens.
- ch. 27 "15. I, Thou, and the Neighborhood" **·** Martin Buber, Jean-Paul Sartre, Augustine of Hippo — I–Thou Relation; Philosophy of Love — James McLachlan pairs Rogers's 'holy ground' between television set and viewer with Buber's turn from ecstatic religion to the everyday after failing the young visitor of 1914 who came to him in need: the I-You relation of full presence versus the I-It of use is what 'It's You I Like' sings. Against Sartre's 'Hell is other people' and Augustine's reading of the burning bush as the omnipotent God, Rogers and Buber (with Rosenzweig's translation of God's name as 'the One who will be present') make listening, presence, and everyday 'twinklings' the substance of neighborly love.
- ch. 28 "16. Loved into Being" **·** Authenticity — Scott Parker argues Fred Rogers converged on Carl Rogers's person-centered approach without ever studying it: genuineness ('The greatest gift you ever give is your honest self'), acceptance (unconditional positive regard: 'I like you just the way you are'), and empathic understanding (the nursery-school doggie-ear exchange) form the facilitative climate that lets children grow toward Kierkegaard's 'that self which one truly is.' With Margaret McFarland's 'attitudes aren't taught, they're caught' and her 'love clay in front of the children,' he shows Mister Rogers as the teacher who liked his viewers into being.
- ch. 29 "17. A Word from a Man Mister Rogers Ruined" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Forgiveness; The Golden Mean — Nicolas Michaud, whose mother was murdered and who asked that her killer get help rather than die, constructs and then refutes the case that Rogers ruined boys by teaching gentleness: against the Thrasymachus line from Republic Book I that justice is for suckers and competition is everything, he argues Rogers's 'three ways to ultimate success: be kind' defines success as happiness; against 'forgiveness is weakness,' he deploys Aristotle's virtue of mildness, being ready to pardon rather than exact penalty, and a rereading of 'turn the other cheek' as claiming equal standing, so that forgiving is strength, not submission.
- ch. 30 "18. Lessons from Fred Rogers’s Dao" **·** Zhuangzi, Laozi — Taoism (Daoism); Wu Wei (effortless action); Authenticity — John Thompson reads Rogers as a Zhuangzian sage without claiming he was a Daoist: the show's spare sets and simple cast embody the uncarved block and Zhuangzi's Dao present 'in the piss and shit' of the everyday; its refusal of 'bombardment' pace is Cook Ding slowly carving the ox and xiaoyaoyou, free and easy wandering, as when X the Owl must wait for Cousin Mary's visit. The post-9/11 'look for the helpers' PSAs, the Burger King parody he publicly rebuffed, and the Emmys ten seconds of silence mark Rogers as a zhenren, a genuine person at home in ziran.
- ch. 31 "19. If Everyone’s Special, … Is Anyone Special" **·** Aristotle, Tom Regan, Socrates — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Unexamined Life — Grace Wehniainen defends 'you are special' against the Fox & Friends 'evil man' charge by separating intrinsic from extrinsic value: on Rogers's 1 Corinthians 12 and Genesis 1:27 reading, worth is God-given and unearned, like the family dog whose napping life has intrinsic value (with Tom Regan's agreement) regardless of tricks. Specialness as 'belonging specifically to a particular person' needs no trophies, only Socratic self-examination before the mirror, Aristotle's true versus vulgar self-love from the Nicomachean Ethics, and Albert Ellis's self-acceptance over performance-based self-esteem.
- ch. 32 "V There Are Many Ways to Solve a Problem" *(front)*
- ch. 33 "20. What Would Mister Rogers Say" **·** Virtue Ethics; Food Ethics — Jennifer Shaw Fischer and Bob Fischer apply Rogers's ideal of 'making goodness attractive' to the 2018 family-separation crisis: knowing his own son's abrupt, unexplained surgical separation caused lifelong trauma, and that his King Friday bomb-scare arc rejects trigger-happy generals for 'Generals of peace,' they argue any policy requiring border agents to lie that children are 'going to a shower' is too ugly to balance our values rightly. Rogers's unpushy vegetarianism ('I don't want to eat anything that has a mother') shows the difference between having a reason and being virtuous: making goodness lovely rather than argumentative.
- ch. 34 "21. Mister Rogers’s Lesson for Democracy" **·** Jürgen Habermas, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Public Sphere; Democracy — Matthew Ussia maps the Trolley's transition between Rogers's house and the Neighborhood of Make-Believe onto Habermas's public sphere: the first-week crisis, Lady Elaine's rearranging of the neighborhood, King Friday's barbed-wire wall and 'Down with the Changes!,' Chef Brockett's humiliation, shows fear collapsing the space where a democracy works through conflict. Like Habermas, who feared television debates would hijack real public talk (and contra Sartre's 'Hell is other people'), Rogers used puppets to say the unsayable, modeling the deliberative space privatized modern life threatens to close.
- ch. 35 "22. Won’t You Be My Comrade" **·** Karl Marx, G.W.F. Hegel — Alienation; Historical Materialism; Class Struggle; Ideology and False Consciousness — Christopher Innes runs Marx's critique of Hegel's idealism against Mister Rogers: the show treats problems (divorce, war, the Clemmons pool scene) ideally, as symbolic gestures rather than material change, much as Hegel's storybook individuals miss money's role. Measured against Capital's alienated worker, 'an appendage to the machine,' contrasted with the suitcase worker who 'knows her work,' and the Communist Manifesto's 'bourgeois socialist' who demands reform not liberation, Rogers emerges as a progressive bourgeois socialist whose make-believe may console children for, or subtly resist, their future exploitation.
- ch. 36 "23. The Neighborhood Is Us" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau — The Problem of Evil; Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society; The General Will — Trip McCrossin frames the show, via Susan Neiman, as Rousseau's answer to the problem of evil: bad things (including bad television) happen to good kids, but education can mitigate evil, which is why Rogers prefers Rousseau's demand to make evil intelligible to Voltaire's Candidean refusal and Pangloss's best-of-all-possible-worlds. Rogers pursued only Emile's second prong, making us as we ought to be by loving children 'just the way they are,' and the post-9/11 PSAs before King Friday's empty castle merge Make-Believe into reality, the last 'modulation' of his thirty-four-year ministry.
- ch. 37 "24. Fred Rogers and the Ethics of Care" **·** Carol Gilligan, Nel Noddings — The Ethics of Care; Caring as the Ground of Ethics — A.G. Holdier places Rogers squarely in the care ethics of Gilligan and Noddings: against Kohlberg's justice stages (the Heinz dilemma recast with Henrietta Pussycat and X the Owl), care means Joan Tronto's four elements of attentiveness, responsibility, competence, and responsiveness, shown in the Clemmons kiddie pool, the Soviet guest understood through an interpreter, and 'just the way you are.' Extending care to animals via Rogers's vegetarianism and Carol Adams's 'absent referent,' and to the self via the closing benediction, he argues Rogers embodied care as particular, embodied practice rather than formula.
- ch. 38 "References" *(notes)*
- ch. 39 "Author Bios" *(notes)*
- ch. 40 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 41 "Index of Episodes" *(notes)*

## Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Monty Python and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy™ Series Editor William Irwin" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "And Where the @#$%^& is the Queen" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Bertrand Russell, David Hume, Albert Camus — Language Games; The Absurd — The editors' introduction recounts Monty Python's 1969 debut and argues the troupe's absurdism bears a deep connection to philosophy because the British Pythons absorbed the Oxford and Cambridge linguistic analysis of Russell, Wittgenstein, Moore, and Ryle while at university in the 1960s. It tours the volume's three parts, previewing each contributor's pairing: Schilbrack reading Life of Brian through Camus's absurd hero, Brighouse using the Argument Clinic for Rawls's analysis of social practices, Asma finding Buddhist mindfulness in The Meaning of Life, Huss pairing the Pythons with Hume on religion, and Spinelli reading sketches through Foucault on the social construction of madness. It concludes there is no single connection between Python and philosophy but many: sketches illuminate philosophy, philosophy illuminates sketches, and Python's empire says something about philosophy's cultural standing (with Wittgenstein's duck-rabbit figuring how the remaining chapters can be seen).
- ch. 7 "Philosophical Aspects of Monty Python" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "“Life’s a Piece of Shit” The Question of Heroism" **·** Albert Camus, David Hume, Immanuel Kant, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus; On Miracles; Bad Faith — Argues Life of Brian is heretical rather than blasphemous: it never mocks Jesus or belief in God but ridicules gullible, smug believing — the Sermon on the Mount crowd mishearing 'blessed are the cheesemakers,' the sandal schism — a critique the chapter aligns with Hume on the appetite for the marvelous and on anthropomorphism. It reads Brian's window sermon ('You're all individuals... think for yourselves') as Kant's Sapere aude and as an existentialist, possibly Christian, humanism. Against the charge of nihilism, it places Brian squarely in Camus's absurd universe (the pointless crucifixion finale and 'Always Look on the Bright Side of Life') and asks whether Brian is an absurd hero like Sisyphus, Meursault, or Dr. Rieux; he is not — he never scorns his fate — so the chapter proposes 'absurd decent guy': Brian lives sincerely, without waiting for miracles, and humor rather than revolt is the counterweight to absurdity.
- ch. 9 "Just Desserts" **·** Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Asks how the exploding-glutton Mr. Creosote sequence in 'The Autumn Years' of The Meaning of Life can provoke laughter rather than horror, given that Creosote shares the monster's marks of physiological impossibility and disgusting category-violation (like Frankenstein's monster or the Alien). The answer: horror requires disgust plus fear, and Creosote, like the slapstick clown, is marked as neither able to harm nor be harmed, so the audience's fear-condition for horror is never met. A second layer of the laughter is vindictive: the maitre d''s wafer-thin mint is retributive justice, a morality-play punishment for gluttony in the lineage of Spenser's Gluttony and Dante's Inferno, so black comedy trades on our sense that the victim deserves what he gets.
- ch. 10 "Meaning and Practice" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, G.E. Moore — Language Games — Uses 'Piston Engine (a Bargain)' from the Hamlet episode of Flying Circus — park-bench women who buy gift-wrapped piston engines because 'it was a bargain,' kill birds with hurled groceries, and end by dazedly reciting Hamlet — to test Wittgenstein's theories of meaning. Both the early Verification Principle and the later meaning-as-use principle fail: we understand the meaning of every sentence yet cannot make sense of what the women are saying, just as 'This is my hand' at the doctor's office, or the philosopher's 'I know that that's a tree' (Wittgenstein's joke at Moore's expense), is meaningful but senseless in context. Drawing on Remarks on Colour and On Certainty, Smith concludes that communal practices and forms of life fix what it makes sense to say, and that the sketch proves Python's Horatio point — 'there are more things in heaven and earth than are dreamt of in your philosophy' — since no theory of meaning captures what makes the exchange funny.
- ch. 11 "Suppose You Were Attached to a Dead Parrot The Role of Thought Experiments" **·** John Rawls, Judith Jarvis Thomson — The Violinist Argument — Takes the Argument Clinic sketch — Mr. Vibrating's pure contradiction versus the customer's demand for 'a connected series of statements intended to establish a proposition' — to argue that paying for good argument is not absurd, because only sustained argument with others gets most of us true beliefs about complex matters. It explains Rawls's method of reflective equilibrium (testing general principles against considered judgments about cases, illustrated by the author's Rimbaud/Rambo censorship blunder) and Judith Jarvis Thomson's violinist thought experiment, showing how such experiments force us to abandon groundless reasons: opponents of abortion who let the violinist go must find grounds other than the fetus's right to life. Good thought experiments, it closes, work like good Python sketches — the Dead Parrot sketch's internally logical absurdity — so a real argument clinic would serve a genuine social function, since interlocutors expose biases that solitary reflection cannot.
- ch. 12 "Getting Right with Brian (Just in Case)" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Henri Bergson, Blaise Pascal — The Death of God; Laughter (the comic as mechanical encrusted on the living); Pascal's Wager; Ressentiment — Reads Life of Brian through Nietzsche's madman: the crowd's laughter at Brian's market sermons ('consider the lilies... have the birds got jobs?') enacts the death of the cheerless, pathos-soaked God, with Brian as a sincere 'divine idiot' who escapes ressentiment by falling idiotically below the dialectic rather than rising above it as an Übermensch. Bergson's account of the comic — rigidity invisible to its bearer, 'as though wearing the ring of Gyges with reverse effect' — explains why the Pythons' straight men, British class consciousness, and the Roman/British empires ('Romani ite domum,' the centurion's Latin lesson) are funny, and why Britons and Romans can laugh at themselves while Americans cannot. Pivoting from Jorge's war on laughter in Eco's The Name of the Rose, the chapter closes with a Pascal's-wager parody: having laughed at Brian, you have already wagered your immortal soul on God being British — the sort of God who can take a joke.
- ch. 13 "Yes, but What About the Killer Rabbit" **·** Parmenides — The Ethics of Care; Gender Performativity; Being and Changelessness — Argues the Pythons invert Arthurian legend's traditional patriarchal function, using Holy Grail — made amid 1970s women's liberation and legal abortion — to expose the absurdity of patriarchy rather than endorse it. The Black Knight's 'None shall pass' embodies an abstract, relationship-blind masculine ethics that the chapter sets against care ethics, while the witch-weighing scene shows Arthur and Bedevere's male bonding eclipsing the mob's victim. Castle Anthrax's 'perilous bed' and the Prince Herbert rescue — Launcelot's heterosexual-matrix heroics collapsing when the damsel in the tower is a prince who enjoys musicals — turn courtly love and gender roles into farce, making the film as much a document of 1970s gender politics as a medieval satire.
- ch. 14 "Mind the Mindfulness" **·** The Buddha, Plato, Augustine of Hippo, Ludwig Wittgenstein — The Four Noble Truths; Non-Self (anatman); Impermanence (anicca); Atman and Brahman — Reads The Meaning of Life as a sustained reductio of transcendentalism — the two-world metaphysics shared by Plato, Augustine, and Vedanta's Brahman/atman — arguing that the film's dehumanizing sketches (the machine that goes 'ping,' the 'every sperm is sacred' father selling his children, the Vegas-style Christmas in Heaven) show how otherworldly belief overrides this-worldly compassion. It parallels the Buddha's scriptural critiques: the Agganna sutta against caste, the no-self (anatta) doctrine against the Bhagavad Gita's soul that licenses Krishna to tell Arjuna killing is a favor, and impermanence (anicca) against the fantasy of eternal bliss. Python's grotesque — Creosote's explosion, the organ-donor lady's 'Galaxy Song' despair — matches Buddhist corpse meditations, while the film steers between hedonism (Creosote) and nihilism (the housewife who surrenders her liver) toward the Buddha's Middle Way and, against everyday distraction (the boardroom's 'people are not wearing enough hats,' the couple who think Schopenhauer begins with an S), toward mindfulness (sati).
- ch. 15 "And Now for . . . Comedic Eliminativism" **·** Socrates, Martin Heidegger, Immanuel Kant, Friedrich Nietzsche, Jacques Derrida, René Descartes — The Meaning of Life; Being-Toward-Death; The Death of God; The Unexamined Life — Argues The Meaning of Life dismantles the 'axial' picture of life as a journey toward a salvific destination (Jaspers's Axial Age thinking), instanced in the headmaster who announces Jenkins's mother's death between Empire Day announcements, the tank fish who never connect Howard's being eaten to their own fate, and the restaurant couple ordering 'philosophy for two' with no appetite for wisdom. The classical answers all fail as delivered: Socrates's philosophy as learning how to die, Heidegger's claim that facing death reveals one's own unique possibilities, and Kant's three questions (What can I know? What should I do? For what may I hope?) collapse into the question of life's meaning, but religion has gone stale and philosophy has become detached trivia. The Pythons instead accomplish the user-friendly domestication of the death of God — the hearty laughter Nietzsche and Derrida counsel — and the chapter coins 'comedic eliminativism' on the model of eliminative materialism's dissolution of Descartes's mind-body problem: replace the yearning for the meaning of life with altered reactions, laughter itself as the solution to the riddle.
- ch. 16 "Aspects of Pythonic Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "Prayer (A Euphemism for Butt-Kissing and Begging)" **·** Socrates, Plato — Euthyphro Dilemma; Faith and Reason; The Problem of Evil — Argues the Pythons' religious gags perform philosophy's preliminary job of challenging doctrine: the 'every sperm is sacred' family makes God a voyeur of contraception, the Life of Brian stoning (rocks flying each time anyone utters 'Jehovah') shows blasphemy law run absurd, and 'Christmas in Heaven' exposes heavenly reward as material compensation. Deploying Socrates and Plato — the Republic's ban on portraying pettiful gods, the Apology on why the virtuous need not fear death, and above all the Euthyphro — the chapter reads the witch-weighing and the Holy Hand Grenade as the ancient problem whether acts are just because God sanctions them, and the chaplain's toadying prayer against God's own 'don't grovel' as proof that sacrifice and prayer are bargaining a perfect being has no need of. The upshot is not atheism but the Socratic verdict that the mobs punishing blasphemy, not the mocked, are the real blasphemers.
- ch. 18 "The Epilogue A Question of Belief" **·** David Hume, Anselm of Canterbury — The Ontological Argument; On Miracles; The Watchmaker Argument (design); Philosophical Skepticism — Systematically pairs Hume's philosophy of religion with Python parodies: Anselm's ontological argument fails because existence cannot be defined into a concept (the Yeti-spotter who never spotted one), with Arthur 'Two Sheds' Jackson, Ron Obvious, and Confuse-A-Cat illustrating the gap between conceivability and possibility; the Galaxy Song's cosmic order and the mock hymn 'All Things Dull and Ugly' stage the design argument and Hume's reply that creation shows moral indifference as readily as benevolence; and Brian's 'miracles' — being 'taken up' then spotted sprinting, curing Simon the hermit by landing on his foot — illustrate Hume's 'Of Miracles' on the unreliability of testimony. Hume's Natural History claim that the cause of religion is fear surfaces in the 'O Father, please don't boil us' hymn and in Arthur's groveling before a God who hates it. Both Hume and the Pythons end in suspended judgment about God — settled, if at all, only by the wrestling match in which 'God exists by two falls to a submission.'
- ch. 19 "Urban Idiots Foucauldian and Pythonesque" **·** Michel Foucault — Power/Knowledge; Discipline and Docile Bodies — Using Foucault's Madness and Civilization, the chapter reads the Flying Circus sketch 'The Idiot in Society' and the 'Hermits' sketch as commentary on madness as a social construct that changes from the medieval tolerance of fools, through the Great Confinement, to modern psychiatric medicalization. Arthur Figgis, the village idiot, is nothing like Foucault's silenced asylum inmates: he speaks rationally to camera about the 'vital psycho-social service' idiots provide, deposits moss at the bank, and lectures in idiocy at the University of East Anglia — madmen who are integrated, have agency, and speak for themselves. The Pythons turn Foucault's picture upside down, since the visibly idiotic are socially integrated while the urban idiots in business suits are the ones confined behind asylum-like walls, and by making idiocy funny they restore the dialogue between reason and unreason that Foucault says the monologue of reason destroyed.
- ch. 20 "Knowledge and Nihilism Science and Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Adam Smith, Karl Marx, Jeremy Bentham — The Death of God; The Golden Mean; Autonomy of the Will; The Invisible Hand — Croskery tours the social institutions that promise guidance for a good life, pairing each with a Python work: Adam Smith's invisible hand and Bentham's greatest-happiness utilitarianism fail in the 'Merchant Banker' sketch, where charity leaves the banker 'a pound down on the whole deal', while Marxist market ideology and alienation surface in the Communist Quiz and the accountant who longs to be a lion tamer. In The Holy Grail, Aristotle's doctrine of the mean sorts Brave Sir Robin's cowardly flight from Sir Lancelot's rash slaughter of a wedding party and Galahad's desire-distorted chastity at Castle Anthrax, with Bedevere's duck-weighing witch logic showing reasoning without judgment, and Arthur's quest collapses because 'strange women lying in ponds handing out swords is no basis for a system of government'. Life of Brian's 'blessed are the cheesemakers' and the 'You're all individuals!' crowd ground a Kantian demand for autonomy against blind obedience to religious rules. The Meaning of Life's 'Galaxy Song' and 'spiraling coils of self-replicating DNA' pose Nietzschean nihilism — science dissolving the highest values — which the film's closing advice to be nice to people and keep a sense of humor answers with a modest, livable meaning.
- ch. 21 "A Nietzschean Conclusion" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus, Friedrich Nietzsche — Bad Faith; The Absurd; Existence Precedes Essence; The Myth of Sisyphus — Slowik argues the Pythons have a positive existentialist message: Kafka's bureaucratic insanity, where ordinary people beat helplessly against irrational rules, recurs in the 'Cheese Shop' and 'Dead Parrot' sketches, and Camus's Sisyphus lives on in the monotonous lives of Palin's city stockbroker and the accountant who dreams of lion taming — repetition without Sisyphus's defiance. The core claim is that Python endorses individual-centered existentialism: Brian's 'You've got to think for yourselves. You're all individuals!' is the troupe's rare direct statement of Sartre's 'existence precedes essence', confirmed by Cleese's and Palin's interviews about resisting those who tell you how to behave, a theme the chapter extends through Nietzsche's critique of moral tradition and organized Christianity. Sartrean bad faith explains Python's stereotyped characters — the aggressive policeman, the pepperpots, and Mr. Praline insisting 'I am not a loony!' while demanding a fish license for his halibut — while Arthur Pewtey's meek 'Right. Right.' and Ron Obvious's physical limits raise nature/nurture objections to Sartrean freedom. The 'Nietzschean Conclusion' is that Monty Python itself exemplifies will to power as 'giving style' to one's character, constantly overcoming its own formulas rather than repeating what succeeded.
- ch. 22 "“Is There Enough of It About ”" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein — Language Games — Carey uses the 'Spectrum: Talking About Things' sketch — where a cricketer is stumped by the question 'What is going on?' and the presenter piles up unanswerable questions — to explain both Wittgensteins as a 'philosopher's cramp' caused by language. Early Wittgenstein's Tractatus holds that sentences picture facts and that attempts to say what makes facts possible are nonsense, so Wittgenstein's own theory is a self-refuting ladder to be climbed and thrown away; the later Wittgenstein instead treats meaning as use, shown through situations A–D where 'What is going on?' makes sense in some contexts and not others, so philosophy has no once-and-for-all cure. Python sketches work the same seam of sense passing into nonsense: interviewing corpses on 'Is There Life After Death?', and a duck, cat, and lizard as mute panel experts, expose how 'talking', 'sitting', 'expressing', and 'having a face' shift meaning with use.
- ch. 23 "So, What Have Philosophers Ever Done for Us" **·** Judith Jarvis Thomson, Peter Singer — The Violinist Argument; The Trolley Problem; The Drowning Child (obligation to aid) — Taylor defends philosophy's bizarre examples against critics like Leon Kass by comparing them to Python's self-reflexive comedy: the 'Complaints' sketch's regress of complaints-about-complaints mirrors how thought experiments make us the audience of our own thinking, as with two coalmine trolley cases that pressure a simple 'minimize pain' utilitarianism toward rule utilitarianism. The 'Police Station' sketch, where it would be better if mad Angus's carnivorous-blancmange story were false, is itself a counterexample to 'always tell the police the truth', and 'The Visitors' stale three-year-old drink invitation undermines the claim that 'inviting in' a fetus creates duties, sharpening Thomson's violinist argument that a right to life does not include a right to another's body. Singer's drowning-child style example and Thomson's violinist show that far-fetched cases clarify practical issues like abortion and famine relief precisely by detaching them from clouding emotion, and the Life of Brian 'What have the Romans ever done for us?' scene supplies the answer: philosophers' examples clarify our views, test them, and are amusing.
- ch. 24 "Pythonic Aspects of Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "Coda" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Martin Heidegger, G.E. Moore, Bertrand Russell, William James, Friedrich Nietzsche — Richardson argues that analytic philosophy is formally identical to absurdist comedy minus the laughter: Carnap's charge that Heidegger's 'Besides Being, there is Nothing' is nonsense becomes, on Richardson's revision, the claim that philosophers are comedians without comic ability, misfiring Gumbys rather than failed musicians. Russell's footnote accusing Hegel of building a system on an unintentional pun and William James's reductio ad humorum against silly philosophical questions are recruited as evidence that philosophical errors begin as jokes no one laughed at. Wittgenstein's saying that the depth of philosophy is the depth of a grammatical joke, together with On Certainty's repeated failure to imagine circumstances in which Moore's 'I know this is my hand' is said with sense, shows the philosopher unknowingly doing stand-up comedy. Python's hijacking and Dennis Moore sketches — criminals who pursue exact philosophical precision about 'nobody move' mid-crime — enact worlds where people genuinely live philosophers' puzzles, so a philosophy that achieved self-consciousness would simply become humor.
- ch. 26 "A Knockout of an Argument" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Gilbert Ryle, Bertrand Russell, Karl Popper — Language Games — Reisch reads Palin's 'Bols Story' presenter — who drowns in ever-finer qualifications about talking, pausing, and gesturing signs — as a parody of Wittgenstein and ordinary language philosophy: brilliant analysis of words that achieves exactly nothing, since he never reaches Holland's most famous aperitif, just as the 'No Time to Lose' advice centre perfects a phrase without touching the failing marriage behind it. The Bruces sketch adds the social critique: the beer-swigging, rule-enforcing Australian department satirizes the cult around Wittgenstein at Cambridge and Oxford and the extra-linguistic forces — Nazism, McCarthyism, anti-communism — that shaped who counted as a philosopher and what got taught. 'The Epilogue' sketch, where a bishop and a philosopher settle God's existence by wrestling until a knockout, suggests philosophical disputes are settled like prizefights by power. Together these form a one-two punch: if fashions, politics, and bullying influence philosophers' beliefs, then philosophy cannot consist exclusively in solving puzzles of ordinary language and must open itself to history and sociology.
- ch. 27 "What Is to Be Done" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Karl Popper — Language Games — A comic persona — an elderly philosopher who claims Wittgenstein stepped on his foot while storming out of the famous poker incident with Popper at the Moral Sciences Club — blames Monty Python for 'destroying' philosophy by popularizing it, mixing it with popular culture, and making it impossible to tell real philosophers from frauds. His prime exhibit is the Dead Parrot sketch, read as a morality play in which no philosopher is ever summoned: Praline and the shopkeeper resolve nothing because amateur, negotiable language is left to haggle over whether the parrot is 'resting' or an ex-parrot, flouting the lesson that language matters. The chapter is itself Python-style satire, and its real target is the gatekeeping picture of philosophy as a serious professionals-only game, ending with the absurd plan to 'depopularize' philosophy by boycotting precisely the kind of popular philosophy book in which it appears.
- ch. 28 "No Shoes for Muskrats How the 1956 Olympic Games Destroyed Indonesian Art" **·** David Hume, W.V.O. Quine — The Web of Belief — Hardcastle recounts how his talk pairing analytic philosophy with Python clips became a touring hit, framing the appeal through Hume's gap between the 'easy and obvious' philosophy that moves people — today's popular culture, including Python — and the 'accurate and abstruse' philosophy that became analytic philosophy. His solution reconceives philosophy as the construction and examination of conceptual schemes rather than a search for truth, with Python supplying what philosophy cannot: conceptual schemes lived from the inside, as when the Dead Parrot shopkeeper embodies Quinean holism by holding that the parrot is alive no matter the evidence, adjusting his other beliefs ('pining for the fjords') to save it, or when 'Nudge Nudge' shows two pub-goers with wholly different schemes chatting without either noticing. We laugh, he concludes, because a new conceptual scheme is by definition unfamiliar and surprising — which is why laughter, unlike disgust, is tied to intelligence, and why philosophy done well is surrounded by the laughter of contemplating what it suggests.
- ch. 29 "“The Cheese Shop,” Episode 33, Monty Python’s Flying Circus, “Salad Days”" **·** W.V.O. Quine, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Albert Camus — The Web of Belief; The Myth of Sisyphus — This is Hardcastle's full talk: analytic philosophy's two revolts map onto Python clips, beginning with the logical positivists' revolt against metaphysics, whose cornerstone verifiability criterion self-destructs because it cannot verify itself. The positivist collapse hands philosophy to Quine's semantic holism — statements face experience 'not individually but only as a corporate body' — which the Dead Parrot sketch enacts as Praline the verificationist checking experiences against the shopkeeper-holist who preserves 'pining for the fjords' by adjusting other statements, and again in the Black Knight, who maintains 'None shall pass' through the loss of every limb. Holism's darker consequence, that no shared axioms are guaranteed so reason cannot found society, appears in the 'Argument Clinic' and in 'Nudge Nudge' as two men effectively speaking different languages in different worlds, while the witch-burning logic illustrates empirically bad human reasoning. The Cheese Shop sketch crowns the continental side — Mr. Mousebender an existentialist hero choosing cheese in an unfeeling world, Mr. Wensleydale the burden of life returning negative answers like Sisyphus's rock — and the Bruces' Philosophers Song is declared the best history of philosophy because it is sung.
- ch. 30 "Everyone Remembers Their First Time About the authors, nearly all of whom have" *(notes)*
- ch. 31 "What Was All That,Then" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "Monty Python and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 33 "Monty Python and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 34 "Copyright Page" *(front)*

## More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "i" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "ii" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Once More into the Time Vortex" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction: it surveys what changed since the first Doctor Who and Philosophy volume (the War Doctor, the Trenzalore death and survival, the Impossible Girl, Dalek divine hatred, the Master becoming 'the Mistress') and previews the volume's questions—whether Clara is possible, whether the Doctor may lie, whether he could have avoided Trenzalore, and whether the Ninth Doctor's 'coward, any day' pacifism gave way to the Twelfth's less-pacifistic cowboy streak. It also introduces the fandom insiders (podcasters, convention runners, a Time Lord Rock musician) who serve as 'Time Lord Presiding' over each Serial, framing the book around the show's emphasis on personal identity and time paradoxes.
- ch. 8 "Serial 1 The Real Never-Ending Story" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Magnetic North" **·** Virtue Ethics; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Siler answers the Twelfth Doctor's question 'Am I a good man?' from 'Into the Dalek' by arguing that goodness is the Doctor's 'magnetic north'—the stable moral orientation his regenerations bend back toward, the force that drove him from Gallifrey's corrupt Time Lords. He concedes a dark side, from the would-be caveman killing of 'An Unearthly Child' to the 'Time Lord Victorious' arrogance of 'The Waters of Mars,' but insists character must be judged over a whole life, including the Doctor's effect on companions like Jo Grant, Leela, Ace, and Rose, whom he teaches 'a better way of livin' your life.' Clara's closing verdict—that he tries to be good and 'that's probably the point'—caps the claim that a settled direction of character, not perfection, makes him a good man.
- ch. 10 "1. A Good Man Goes to War" **·** Virtue Ethics; The Ethics of Political Violence — Pless argues the Doctor's shift from the Ninth's self-avowed 'coward, any day' to the Eleventh's gun-toting action hero tracks real-world politics and markets rather than internal story logic: after the 7/7 London bombings and amid the War on Terror, and as the show's global export grew, a war-weary British ideal gave way to the decisive 'Oncoming Storm.' She traces the arc through the Tenth's gleeful xenocide of the Racnoss in 'The Runaway Bride,' the eternal punishment of the Family of Blood, the Eleventh brainwashing humanity to exterminate the Silence in 'Day of the Moon,' and the assault of 'A Good Man Goes to War,' before 'The Day of the Doctor' retcons the Time War so the Doctor never destroyed the Time Lords, validating the action-hero persona. Her conclusion: in a crisis culture demanding proactive heroes, cowardice—once the Doctor's honest self-assessment—was rebranded as vice.
- ch. 11 "2. How Time Lords Invented TV" *(no index entry yet)* — Dray reads Doctor Who as a metaphor for television itself: the Doctor and his box emerge from a junkyard just after FCC chairman Newton Minow called TV a 'vast wasteland,' and the show turns the medium's supposed weaknesses—shaky effects, departing actors, budget limits—into its fiction, most famously converting William Hartnell's failing health into regeneration. Following 'An Unearthly Child' through the cancellation-era New Adventures novels, the flawed 1996 TV movie, and the Davies and Moffat eras (including Amy literally believing the erased Doctor back into existence in 'The Big Bang'), he argues television's iterative, audience-entangled, endlessly rewritable nature is the show's real subject. The TARDIS, 'bigger on the inside,' is television itself, and 'The Day of the Doctor' celebrates a medium that can remake the old anew—self-interrogating its own dangers in stories like 'The Idiot's Lantern' and 'Bad Wolf.'
- ch. 12 "3. The Mystical Alchemy of “Midnight”" *(no index entry yet)* — Sas uses literary alchemy's three-stage magnum opus to read 'Midnight' as the nigredo—the black stage of dissolution that begins the Tenth Doctor's arc of purification, death, and rebirth ending in his regeneration in 'The End of Time.' She shows Russell T Davies loading the episode with nigredo imagery: the deadly Xtonic sunlight that calcinates bodies to ash, the planet of endless 'midnight' and witching-hour folklore, the Salem-style mob panic modeled on The Crucible as the mimicking Sky drives the passengers to demand a sacrificial victim, and the Doctor stripped of TARDIS, companion Donna, authority, and finally his voice. The Doctor's humbling—he solves nothing and is saved only by the Hostess's self-sacrifice—purges the ego that later swells into 'Time Lord Victorious,' while his reunion with the fiery Donna foreshadows the alchemical fusion of the DoctorDonna and eventual rebirth.
- ch. 13 "4. How Possible Is the Impossible Girl" **·** Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, Aristotle, Plato — Personal Identity; The Unconscious; Archetypes; The Collective Unconscious — Smith asks how one Clara can exist as Oswin the converted Dalek, a Victorian governess, and a present-day nanny, and answers with philosophy of mind: after the real Clara steps into the Doctor's timeline on Trenzalore, the 'echoes' are best understood as manifestations within the Doctor's own subconscious, read through Freud's dream interpretation and id-ego-superego (the echoes act as his conscience) and Jung's archetypes, collective unconscious, individuation, and synchronicity—her name meaning clarity, her red wardrobe marking the copies, and the leaf of 'The Rings of Akhaten' as the meaningful coincidence that produced her. Aristotle's Categories frames what Oswin still shares with humanity after Dalek conversion, and the soufflé-is-the-recipe line together with social-cognition research on multiple selves supports the conclusion that the Claras are metaphysically the same person despite different bodies and roles—making the 'Impossible Girl' possible.
- ch. 14 "5. Every Lonely Monster Needs a Companion" **·** Aristotle, Plato, David Hume — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Is–Ought Problem; The Ethics of Care — Gadsden asks why a near-omnipotent Time Lord needs companions at all and tests four hypotheses against his solo meltdowns—executing Solomon in 'Dinosaurs on a Spaceship,' nearly murdering Jex in 'A Town Called Mercy,' and declaring himself 'Time Lord Victorious' in 'The Waters of Mars.' He rejects the Lord Acton power-corrupts hypothesis via Glaucon's ring story in Plato's Republic, since powerless companions offer no threat of reprisal or dishonor, and qualifies J.J. Sylvia's care-ethics 'empathetic link' because the Doctor cares for non-human species like the Star Whale too. He favors two answers: Hume's fact/value gap as a millennium-long moral myopia ('I can't see it anymore,' the deleted 'Flesh and Stone' confession), and Aristotle's point in the Nicomachean Ethics that only virtuous friends—moral peers who mirror us—can expose the Doctor's blind spots, like his 'God Complex.'
- ch. 15 "Serial 2 Mind-Bending Impossibility-Shattering Jammie Dodgers" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "You’re Fantastic!" **·** Potentiality and Actuality — Viguié's Serial 2 preface argues the show's ultimate philosophy is 'you're fantastic': the Doctor takes people yearning for something more—Rose the shop girl becoming Bad Wolf, Rory becoming the Last Centurion, Donna the temp becoming in a way the Doctor herself—and actualizes potential they never believed they had. He applies the lesson to his own life, describing how the show's belief in untapped human potential pushed him from a soul-sucking job to creating his Doctor Geek's Laboratory STEM-outreach audio show and Science Fair, urging readers to answer the Doctor's call and live up to what the Fourth Doctor called our 'inventive, invincible, indomitable' species' promise.
- ch. 17 "6. Weeping Angels and Many Worlds" **·** Aristotle — Free Will vs Determinism; The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Possible Worlds — Sutton argues the causal loops of 'Blink' and 'The Angels Take Manhattan' need not destroy libertarian free will: the Doctor's claim that a known future is 'written in stone' conflates ordinary foreknowledge, which leaves agents free to make the knower wrong, with infallible knowledge that only exists because the act occurs. Adapting Hugh Everett's many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics to free choices, he shows how branching timelines let the Doctor read Melody Malone, decline to break River's wrist, and still close the loop—some parallel Doctor does what the book records—while Aristotle's future contingents in De Interpretatione secure the indeterminacy of what 'will' happen. Answering the objection that branch-splitting is really fatalism, he appeals to the subjective viewpoint (what matters is 'my me'), explains how Kathy and Billy's messages in 'Blink' reach Sally on at least one branch, and solves why the Doctor is always so lucky: we follow the one branch where he survives.
- ch. 18 "7. What the Doctor Can and Can’t Change" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Compatibilism; Fate and Foreknowledge — Delamont codifies the Whoniverse's four rules of time travel—time can be rewritten, fixed points cannot, knowing your future fixes it, and crossing your own timeline should be avoided—from cases like 'The Waters of Mars' (Adelaide's suicide restoring the fixed outcome), 'The Angels Take Manhattan' (Rory vanishing at the sight of his gravestone), 'Father's Day,' and 'The Girl Who Waited.' She then asks whether the Doctor could have avoided Trenzalore and argues the universe is hard-deterministic once amended with the laws of time travel, since rules 2–4 constrain action the way soft determinism's freedom from external forces would not allow. Tracing the causal dominoes back from the truth-field question through the Silence, River's creation, the Pandorica, and the Time Lords' pocket-universe broadcast to the crack in Amy's wall, she concludes he could not have avoided Trenzalore short of unwriting his entire history—'you can't change history if you're part of it.'
- ch. 19 "8. Could the Doctor Have Avoided Trenzalore" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Possible Worlds; Fate and Foreknowledge — Pigliucci treats the two Trenzalore timelines of 'The Name of the Doctor' and 'The Time of the Doctor' as allohistory—an if-then counterfactual in Livy's tradition about Alexander the Great—and argues Everettian many-worlds quantum mechanics best explains how the Time Lords' one decision (granting or withholding a new regeneration cycle) can go both ways across parallel worlds. Rejecting contra-causal free will as a theological leftover, he prefers the cognitive scientist's 'volition' and defends compatibilism: the split stems from ordinary quantum-random interaction during deliberation, not magic, so the Doctor's choices are real without violating physics. Distinguishing fate from free will via Oedipus and the Doctor's 'Destiny Trap,' he concludes the Doctor was fated to make his last stand on Trenzalore as a fixed point in time, while the outcome of the siege depended on a genuine choice that, as David Deutsch puts it, thickened the stack of universes where good things happen.
- ch. 20 "9. How the Doctor Knows" **·** René Descartes, Alvin Goldman, Charles Sanders Peirce, Plato — Brain in a Vat; Reliabilism; Methodological Doubt (evil demon); The Cogito — Smithka argues the Doctor is a reliabilist about knowledge rather than a Cartesian strong foundationalist: using 'Amy's Choice,' 'The Beast Below' (the glass of water, the engine room, Amy's inference that the Star Whale came willingly), 'Silence in the Library' (the chicken-leg experiment implicating the Vashta Nerada), and Davros's Dalek trials in 'Genesis of the Daleks,' she shows him trusting perception in the right causal chain and reasoning inductively and abductively—Peirce's inference to the best explanation—instead of demanding Cartesian certainty. Against Descartes's dream and evil-genius skepticism, updated as Putnam-style brain-in-a-vat scenarios via the Dream Crabs of 'Last Christmas' and the Dream Lord's two-worlds game, she deploys Goldman's three criteria for perceptual knowledge: justification is packed into reliable belief-forming processes, and doubt is warranted only in known abnormal contexts like funhouses or Dream Lord games.
- ch. 21 "10. One Good, Solid Hope—the Impossible Girl" **·** John Locke, Plutarch — Personal Identity (memory theory); Ship of Theseus; Personal Identity — Elsby and Luzecky ask what stays constant across Clara's echoes and argue traditional identity theories fail her: Locke's memory-continuity and same-life account cannot apply because no echo remembers the others, and Plutarch's Ship of Theseus—invoked by the Doctor's broom speech in 'Deep Breath'—rules out bodily continuity, since the echoes have different bodies and minds. Their positive view is that Clara is less a particular than a universal, a 'recipe' or species whose instances share an essence ('the soufflé isn't the soufflé; the soufflé is the recipe'), with the modern-day Clara 'real' as the origin of the echoes. That essence, shown in climbing the ladder to the clouds in 'The Snowmen,' facing the parasite-god with the most important leaf in human history in 'The Rings of Akhaten,' stepping into the Doctor's torn timeline in 'The Name of the Doctor,' and persuading the Time Lords in 'The Time of the Doctor,' is hope itself.
- ch. 22 "11. What the Soufflé Girl Could Teach Descartes" **·** René Descartes, Sigmund Freud, Hilary Putnam, Alan Turing, Gilbert Ryle — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Mind–Body Dualism; Brain in a Vat; The Turing Test — Becker-Lindenthal uses 'Amy's Choice' to revise Descartes's dream skepticism: the Dream Lord is not an external evil demon but the Doctor's own repressed alter ego fed by psychic pollen, so the self-delusion Descartes dismissed becomes the real deceiver, read through Freud's Interpretation of Dreams (Rory's death as the Doctor's wish, Amy's choice as Thanatos). She then reads Oswin in 'Asylum of the Daleks' as a brain-in-a-vat variant (Putnam's Reason, Truth and History) with a crucial difference—Oswin hacks the Dalek program and follows her own agenda—so her self-deceptive soufflé-baking fantasy is a self-formation that preserves her 'I' inside Dalek hardware, complicating Ryle's rejection of the ghost in the machine. Finally, the Doctor judges Oswin by a Turing test plus Putnam's test of reference (the impossible milk and eggs), but her self-deception is vindicated when it lets her save the Doctor and the universe.
- ch. 23 "12. How to Build a TARDIS" **·** The Metaphysics of Time Travel — Physicists Tippett and Tsang lay out a real general-relativistic 'TARDIS'—a Traversable Achronal Retrograde Domain in Spacetime: a bubble of curvature carrying occupants around a closed loop through space and time, with outside observers seeing two bubbles, one evolving forwards and one backwards, and interior events bound by Novikov's self-consistency condition. After touring the Alcubierre warp drive, Morris-Thorne wormholes with their twin-paradox time offset, the Tipler cylinder's frame dragging, and the Grandfather Paradox (with 'Father's Day' and 'Genesis of the Daleks' as illustrations), they show their geometry requires exotic, gravitationally repulsive faster-than-light matter violating the classical energy conditions. Splicing cut TARDIS segments could connect any two events in space and time, and a half-TARDIS would send its traveler emerging backwards in time as antimatter, as when Omega converts the Doctors in 'The Three Doctors.'
- ch. 24 "Serial 3 Values in the Time Vortex" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "The Doctor Who Masculine Romantic Ideal" *(no index entry yet)* — Spivey's Serial 3 preface proposes 'The Doctor Who Masculine Romantic Ideal': female fans are drawn to the Doctor's humor under fire (the banana daiquiri, the tie wrapped round his head), his lively intellect, and his 'broken while unattainable' past—the post-Time-War scars that kept him aloof from Rose, and the sense that he is a damaged man worth saving. Writing from his background in interpersonal communication and his experience as a Gallifrey-inspired rock musician dubbed 'Sexiest Man in Tampa Bay,' he argues the Doctor's appeal transfers by association to fandom men who share these traits, and that bookish 'cool savants' overlooked by traditional masculinity can cultivate this ideal—humor, intellect, and honorable wounds—as a genuine romantic alternative.
- ch. 26 "13. Should the Doctor Eat His Companions" **·** Jeremy Bentham — Utilitarianism; Speciesism; Food Ethics — Littmann turns the Doctor-companion relationship into a mirror for animal ethics: since the Doctor stands to humans as we stand to animals—deciding for Rose without asking in 'The End of the World,' implanting nanorecorders unconsented in 'Day of the Moon'—every standard justification for our treatment of animals (might makes right, superior intelligence, natural predation) would equally license him to eat Clara cutlets, yet he instead defends humanity from Daleks, Cybermen, and naturally predatory species like the Weeping Angels, the Minotaur, and the Swarm. Finding no non-arbitrary place to draw the intelligence line—what of the human-level gangers, the enslaved Ood, or mentally disabled humans?—he endorses Bentham's utilitarian suffering standard from 'Can they suffer?', concluding that eating humans fails the utilitarian test because the pleasure cannot outweigh a whole life's happiness, and that whether eating meat passes that same test is the question our own treatment of animals must answer.
- ch. 27 "14. The Doctor’s Desire for Human Suffering" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, John Stuart Mill — Amor Fati (love of fate); Will to Power; The Last Man — Cooper reads 'Rise of the Cybermen' and 'The Age of Steel' as staging Nietzsche against Mill's pain-eradicating utilitarianism: John Lumic, who builds the Cybermen to abolish his sickness, exemplifies the life-denying herd—losing his creativity, craving 'unity and uniformity,' becoming 'a living brain with a heart of steel'—while the Doctor, answering that a life without pain would be 'you might as well kill me,' affirms suffering as the source of creativity, striving, and strength. She extends the Nietzschean reading to the Doctor's character: his guilt over the Time War double-genocide and his loneliness ('the only certainty left is that you'll end up alone') become the pain that makes him merciful, from offering Dalek Caan compassion after 'Evolution of the Daleks' to forgiving the Master in 'Last of the Time Lords,' so that mercy is, as the Genealogy of Morals says, 'the privilege of the most powerful man.'
- ch. 28 "15. The Way of the Doctor Is Deception" **·** Immanuel Kant, Jeremy Bentham, Plato, Bernard Williams, Aristotle, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Noble Lie; The Categorical Imperative; Respect for Persons; Utilitarianism — Dodge takes Rule #1 - the Doctor lies - through the major theories of lying: Bernard Williams's definition (asserting what you believe false with intent to deceive), Aristotle's claim that all lies are base, Kant's categorical imperative and respect for persons (even the Vinvocci's shimmer disguises in 'The End of Time' abuse trust), and Bentham's pleasure-pain calculus, which condemns the faked death at Lake Silencio ('The Impossible Astronaut') for the grief it caused Amy and Rory yet rewards the greater happiness it made possible. Against the absolutists he sets Plato's Noble Lie from the Republic - the elite falsehood that keeps society functioning - as what the Doctor emulates by deceiving the universe into thinking him dead ('The Wedding of River Song'), and Nietzsche's point in Human, All Too Human that lying is ethically neutral when the pretense is sustainable, as when the Doctor hides the ganger-Amy switch from Rory ('The Almost People'). The upshot: the Doctor's lies are wrong in themselves but routinely justified by the good they do, which is why sometimes the hero lies.
- ch. 29 "16. Divine Hatred—Dalek Beauty" **·** Immanuel Kant, Plato, Friedrich Nietzsche, David Hume, Arthur Schopenhauer — Theory of Forms; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Bowman uses 'Asylum of the Daleks' - where the Daleks preserve broken, insane Daleks as embodiments of 'divine hatred' - to test whether beauty is objective or subjective. Plato's Theory of Forms explains how hatred could be beautiful (the more a thing instantiates its Form, the more beautiful it is), while the Hume-Kant antinomy of beauty, Kant's disinterested judgment of taste (illustrated by Rory and Amy's invested judgments of each other versus the TARDIS's detached 'pretty'), and Nietzsche's account of beauty leading to divinity frame the Dalek hive mind's shared conceptual scheme. Since Kant says beauty is a symbol of morality, the Asylum-as-museum reveals Dalek values - which is why human-on-the-inside Clara is enshrined under maximum security, and why the Doctor is sickened to learn that he is himself an object of Dalek beauty.
- ch. 30 "17. The Friends of a Time Lord" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Littmann applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics taxonomy of friendship - pleasure, usefulness, and mutual goodness - to fifty years of Doctor-companion pairings, from the Hartnell Doctor's glee touring Vortis with Ian to New Series companions chosen as friends who routinely save the day, from Barbara's Dalek revolt to Clara saving every incarnation of the Doctor. He argues Aristotle would still judge the Doctor's friendships defective: they are short-lived, unequal in station, intellect, and morality, and the companions cannot know him well enough (not even his name) for the perfect friendship of the good. Littmann then corrects Aristotle on two counts: friends need not be moral experts to serve as moral critics (Rose in 'Dalek,' Amy in 'A Town Called Mercy'), and the Doctor's favoritism toward his companions - risking worlds to save them, as when Rory weighs Amy's life against the universe in 'The Big Bang' - shows that preferring friends over strangers is itself his most frequent moral failing.
- ch. 31 "18. Sex for Dummies, Humans, and Time Lords" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Lewis argues the New Series' sexual revolution (Captain Jack, Vastra and Jenny, the Doctor's multiple marriages) teaches that any relationship between rational, autonomous, consenting adults is morally permissible. Building on John Corvino's defense of homosexual sex, he dismantles the 'unnatural means immoral' argument definition by definition (unusual, not practiced by animals, contrary to innate desire, contrary to natural purpose or divine intent, disgusting), rejects the empirical slippery slope as a fallacy, and uses Whoniverse cases - young Amelia Pond's non-autonomous choice to leave with the Doctor, the Slitheen pig as mere causal agent, manipulation that would undermine informed consent - to show that only autonomy grounds sexual morality. Objections to same-sex or human-alien relationships turn out to confuse the aesthetic ('ugly') with the ethical ('wrong').
- ch. 32 "19. The Doctor is a (Wo)Man!" **·** Simone de Beauvoir, Judith Butler — One Is Not Born a Woman; Gender Performativity — Kellen asks whether the Doctor could regenerate as a woman, marshaling the canon evidence (the Corsair's lives as both sexes, the Sisterhood of Karn offering 'man or woman,' Missy) to show biology poses no obstacle - clownfish and rare human sex changes make the point mundane. Against Peter Davison's claim that a female Doctor 'doesn't work,' he deploys Simone de Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' and Judith Butler's account in Gender Trouble of gender as a stylized repetition of acts performed over time, arguing the Doctor already performs care-ethicist, 'feminine' roles and could just as well perform female ones. Since regeneration routinely transforms personality without ending the Doctor, the only remaining objection is bias toward a supposedly male core identity.
- ch. 33 "Serial 4 Gallifrey Falls No More" *(front)*
- ch. 34 "Terrifying, and Mad, and Bloody Brilliant" *(no index entry yet)* — Hennessee's interlude is a fan memoir told in cuts between 1984, 1994, 2004, and 2014: discovering Tom Baker's Doctor at twelve, dropping fandom as a New York undergraduate, and finding community again through a bookstore corkboard meeting and the 2005 revival. It shows rather than argues that Doctor Who is life-shaping - informing its fan's morality, tastes, friendships, and speculations about time, free will, and the self - while asking whether the boy of 1984 would recognize the man of 2014. It closes by refusing to separate the show from life: both are 'terrifying, and mad, and bloody brilliant.'
- ch. 35 "20. The Doctor Lies" **·** Immanuel Kant, Augustine of Hippo, Plato, Henry Sidgwick — The Noble Lie; The Categorical Imperative; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — McCain distinguishes lying (directly asserting what you believe false to make another believe it) from mere deception - the Sixth Doctor feeding Jamie false information for Sontaran Stike to overhear in 'The Two Doctors' deceives without lying - then asks whether the Doctor can lie to himself, answering that incarnations can lie to later selves (the Eleventh's suspicious 'I have absolutely no idea' about the children on Gallifrey in 'The Day of the Doctor') but a current self cannot. The stakes are moral: against Kant's and Augustine's absolute prohibition of lying, Plato's Republic and Sidgwick's Methods of Ethics defend noble lies, and Robert C. Solomon's view of self-deception as coping with the unbearable suggests that if the Doctor did engineer himself to forget the Time War genocide - as Ten and Wilf did to Donna in 'Journey's End' - it might be a good man's forgivable way of going on.
- ch. 36 "21. Forgetting Is the Human Superpower" **·** Sigmund Freud — The Unconscious; Personal Identity — Seymour reads the War-through-Eleventh Doctors through Freud's notion of Afterwardness (Nachtraeglichkeit) from Studies on Hysteria - memory is continually reforged as new information recontextualizes the past - so that learning Gallifrey was saved in 'The Day of the Doctor' changes not the Doctor but his memories of himself, turning penance into hope. She traces each Self constructed from Time War memory: Nine's guilt exploited by the Gelth and voiced in 'Boom Town' ('Only a killer would know that'), Ten's hubris once he forgets what he is capable of ('Time Lord Victorious' in 'The Waters of Mars'), and Eleven's danger when the memory fades and companions must remind him who he is ('A Town Called Mercy'). The chapter concludes the Doctor must keep the memory of his regret to keep being the Doctor - Clara's 'What you've always done. Be a doctor.'
- ch. 37 "22. The Mnemotechnics of Amy Pond" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Holdier explains how Amy remembering the Doctor back into existence at her wedding ('The Big Bang') could work, combining Nietzsche's mnemotechnics from the second essay of On the Genealogy of Morals - only that which never ceases to hurt stays in the memory - with J.R.R. Tolkien's 'On Fairy-Stories,' whose internally coherent secondary worlds sustain cultural memory and 'recover' a clear view of reality. On this reading the Doctor deliberately plants his painful loss in Amy's subconscious wrapped in a fairy tale; Amy is the ideal medium because she lacked the willpower to hold onto Rory when the cracks rewrote her ('Cold Blood'), yet her fairy-tale-soaked childhood beside the Crack in her wall let the Doctor's last story germinate into the words that returned the TARDIS to the universe.
- ch. 38 "23. Failing and Forgiving in the Name of the Doctor" **·** Forgiveness; Personal Identity; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Hoffman reads the Doctor's banishment of the War Doctor ('Doctor no more,' his actions 'not done in the name of the Doctor') as a failure of self-forgiveness driven by what Jeffrie Murphy calls the moral hatred of self and Robin Dillon the 'self-as-feared,' rather than mere guilt over the genocide of Gallifrey. Drawing on the self-forgiveness literature (Blustein, Griswold, Westlund), he argues that 'The Day of the Doctor' shows forgiveness neither excuses nor extinguishes blame: the Tenth and Eleventh Doctors forgive their past self by recognizing he shared their Doctorly motives and was forced into an impossible choice. Clara's outsider faith ('be a doctor') supplies the third-party affirmation that dissolves the identity-destroying dilemma and frees the Doctor to find the third option that saves Gallifrey.
- ch. 39 "24. Who’s Duty to Whom" **·** Immanuel Kant, Thomas Hobbes, David Hume — The Categorical Imperative; Reason Is the Slave of the Passions; The Social Contract; The State of Nature — Dawson asks why the Doctor sides with humans and humanoids against rational non-humanoids, testing Kant first: a logic-grounded categorical morality can count the Daleks as immoral rather than amoral (universalized slavery is incoherent), but pure reason cannot motivate Daleks or the Master, and Kant's theory absurdly condemns the Doctor's lies and his theft of the TARDIS. Hobbesian psychological egoism and the social contract fare worse - the Daleks are no co-signatories, and self-sacrifices from Katarina to the Doctor's seemingly final years on Trenzalore resist the egoist's retelling - so the chapter lands with Hume: sympathy and benevolence found morality on feeling, which explains and partly excuses the Doctor's parochial partiality for beings who resemble him, making him 'at least half-Humean.'
- ch. 40 "25. Meeting Up with Your Self" **·** Gilles Deleuze, John Locke — Personal Identity (memory theory); Existentialism — Sylvia and Stevens use Doctor Who's crossover episodes to complicate the Self-Other distinction: existentially (via Yalom and Maslow), the Doctor's name-promise - 'never cruel or cowardly... never give up, never give in' - supplies meaning, while Ten and Eleven must stop treating the War Doctor as Other. Deleuze's account of learning through the shock of encountering the Other structures the reading of 'The Girl Who Waited,' where young Amy and her thirty-six-years-older self form an assemblage in which the older Amy relearns her love for Rory and chooses annihilation for his sake. Locke's memory theory of personal identity frames the puzzle that a version of you with different memories may be an Other, which the authors extend to confronting our recorded past selves on social media and learning empathy from the shock.
- ch. 41 "26. Time Lords Are Us" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty — Phenomenology; Embodiment (the lived body) — Elder argues the 'back to front' love story of the Doctor and River Song - her past is his future, as at Lake Silencio - refutes both the objective 'river' model of time and the subjective 'song' model on which the mind assembles moments like notes into a flow. Following Merleau-Ponty, he grounds the experience of flow in pre-reflective embodied perception: Clara's walk around the TARDIS and her 'it's smaller on the outside' show a finite body gripping a multifaceted world, so that 'time is the subject and the subject is time.' Because temporalities, unlike private consciousnesses, can intertwine in a shared present, the Doctor and River can build a relationship out of each other's pasts and futures - and in this sense we are all Time Lords.
- ch. 42 "More Matrix of Time-Lord Bibliographic Sources" *(notes)*
- ch. 43 "The Second Great Gallifreyan High Council" *(notes)*
- ch. 44 "Higher-Order Logical Index for the Cyberman and Dalek in All of Us" *(notes)*
