- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Red Rising and Philosophy" **·** Class Struggle; The Meaning of Life — The editors' introduction argues that Red Rising grips because it mirrors our own world of class struggle, where a Gold-like elite lives in luxury on the backs of oppressed laborers kept distracted by games and propaganda. It traces Darrow's arc from resigning himself to death after Eo's execution, through his carving and campaign of destruction, to the discovery that friendship with Sevro, Mustang, Victra, and Ragnar—not revenge—is what actually pulls him out of life's mines. It closes by previewing the volume's questions: whether enhancement could doom humanity, whether Darrow is the same person after the carving, love versus vengeance, how society should be structured, and the meaning of life.
- ch. 8 "I. Conundrums for the Quality Control Board" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "1. When Evolution Strikes Back" **·** Social Darwinism; Class Struggle — Tim Jones argues the Golds misread Darwin: they take themselves to be the perfected endpoint of natural selection and use the Passage and Institute to 'help Nature along' by culling weaker Golds, justifying the subjugation of lower Colors—the same social-Darwinist logic Hitler and Stalin used to dress up atrocity. Using Darwin's own contrast between natural selection and man-made selective breeding, he shows the Institute is an artificial arena and the Golds' shaping of Reds and Pinks is self-serving husbandry, not nature's work. The twist is that the very traits the Golds bred into lowReds—Helldiver knuckles, miner's endurance, drill-floor courage—are what win Darrow the Institute, the Iron Rain, and the fight against the Jackal, so their manipulated evolution becomes the tool of their own extinction, just as Quicksilver's case against the static Color hierarchy implies.
- ch. 10 "2. Not So Human After All" **·** Aristotle, Peter Singer — Speciesism — Brendan Shea takes the Jackal's claim that Golds and Reds are separate species (Homo flameus versus Homo sapiens) seriously and tests it first against Aristotle's essentialism—species fixed by necessary properties, complete with the doctrine of natural slaves—and then against three modern species concepts (Mayr's interbreeding criterion, the phylogenetic common-ancestry view, and the ecological-niche view), showing each gives the Jackal ambiguous or inconvenient verdicts, from sterile Pinks to horizontal gene transfer. He concludes with Peter Singer that moral equality never depended on equal intelligence or strength: Reds have interests just as Golds do, so enslaving them would be wrong even if Adrius were right about the biology. The deeper lesson is that the Jackal reasoned backwards from his commitment to Gold rule, finding whatever differences his prejudice needed—a warning against 'discovering' biological support for pre-existing biases.
- ch. 11 "3. Hero or Villain" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill, Jeremy Bentham — Consequentialism; Virtue Ethics; Humanity as an End in Itself — Kevin McCain asks whether Darrow the hero and Nero au Augustus the villain can really be told apart, noting both hold noble goals (Eo's dream versus preserving humanity) and share brutal means. Consequentialism fails to separate them: Darrow's sacrifice of dockworkers and Sons of Ares to Romulus mirrors Nero's 'I do what I need to do to protect the greater good,' and Harmony's sacrificing Evey shows the same ends-justify-means reasoning. Kantian ethics condemns both, since each lies to people and sacrifices them without consent, treating them as mere means to an end. Virtue ethics finally offers grounds: Aristotle's requirement of proper motivation, developed through Michael Slote, distinguishes Darrow, who acts from love for Eo, his friends, and the Colors and is wracked by guilt, from Nero, who is fueled by inhuman pride and feels nothing at Eo's hanging—so motivation may be what makes one forgivable and the other a villain, though the chapter ends wondering if good intentions pave the road to Hell.
- ch. 12 "4. Raising Darrow" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau — The Problem of Evil; The General Will; Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society — Trip McCrossin reads Darrow's storyline as an engagement with the problem of evil in both its theological form (Harmony dubbing him Lazarus, the parables of John and Luke) and its secular form, which Susan Neiman traces to the Rousseau-Voltaire dispute: must evil be made intelligible or not? Darrow begins Voltairean—incredulous before the rigged Laurel and Eo's hanging ('She left me')—but his resurrection and political awakening on the surface remake him Rousseauian: evil is the misalignment of individual and general wills, and humans are corrupted by society, not born bad. The chapter reads Darrow's 'Man was born free' broadcast in Morning Star, his new social contract with Victra, and the education of Pax (with Lysander left to Cassius to 'raise him right') as Rousseau's Social Contract and Emile program—break the chains, then educate each generation so its contracts align ever closer with the general will.
- ch. 13 "5. The One, the Only, Darrow" **·** John Locke, Plutarch — Personal Identity; Ship of Theseus; Personal Identity (memory theory); Teleporter Paradox (personal fission) — Kevin McCain uses Darrow's transformations—Helldiver of Lykos, carved Gold lancer, Reaper of Mars—to ask what makes him numerically the same person, warming up with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus replayed on the Pax and the Quinn trading parts. Same-matter and animalist views (Eric Olson) struggle with Mickey's near-total carving and Darrow's restarted heart, and Locke's prince-and-cobbler example, run as a carver swapping Darrow's and the Jackal's psychologies, sinks all physical-continuity views. The simple memory theory breaks transitivity across Darrow's childhood, and Sydney Shoemaker's psychological-continuity fix then fails when a carver splits Darrow's brain into two surviving bodies—a fission case where both new Darrows continue him—while the soul view cannot be verified; the chapter ends with Trenton Merricks's suggestion that there may be no criteria of identity over time at all.
- ch. 14 "II. Searching for Eo’s Dream" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "6. Driven by Love to Go to War" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Aristotle — Philosophy of Love; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society — John Karavitis deploys Alain Badiou's account of love as a contingent encounter founding the 'Two scene'—seeing the world from the perspective of difference—to argue that Darrow and Eo were never truly in love: their glade conversation, his 'nobility of obedience' against her 'live for more,' was two monologues, and you cannot love a memory. He then diagnoses Darrow as a narcissist in Rousseau's sense of amour-propre—self-love turned vanity that lies to itself—whose quest serves to manage his shame at failing to protect Eo, citing Erich Fromm on narcissism's path to fascism and Aristotle on habituation into Gold ways. Only the Jackal's stone-table imprisonment shatters the narcissism ('Man is no island'), letting Darrow embrace agape, with Ovid's Echo and Narcissus and the haemanthus framing the trilogy as a warning against self-love.
- ch. 16 "7. Being for Red" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, David Hume, René Descartes, Plato, Sigmund Freud — Bad Faith; Existence Precedes Essence; The Look (hell is other people); Bundle Theory of Self — Courtland Lewis asks who Darrow is—Red, Gold, hybrid, savior—and surveys theories of the self: Plato's immortal soul ruling the body, Descartes's cogito as thinking thing, and Hume's denial that introspection ever reveals more than a stream of perceptions (we never experience a soul, only thinking). Freud's id-ego-superego offers a secular soul, but Sartre carries the chapter: Darrow is being-for-itself, perpetually projecting what he is not, tortured by the Look of others—Eo seeing a savior, Mustang holding him at gunpoint, Roque's betrayed friendship—and prone to bad faith through 'guardrails' like the Vale, excuses about Eo and Uncle Narol, and pining for Mustang instead of owning his choice. Since existence precedes essence, Darrow is nothing but the sum of his free choices, and to live otherwise is to choose slavery.
- ch. 17 "8. Living for More" **·** Susan Wolf, Albert Camus, Thomas Nagel — The Meaning of Life; Meaning in Life; The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus — Kevin McCain separates meaning of life—why humans exist at all, with no creator-God found in Gold nihilism ('the Golds have no God'), the Obsidians' manufactured Norse religion, or the Reds' Vale and Old Man—from meaning in life, following Susan Wolf's distinction. After rejecting supernaturalism and pessimistic naturalism (Nero's universe that 'does not notice us,' met by Karnus's Camus-like defiant pride and Thomas Nagel's ironic stance), he rejects Richard Taylor's subjectivism via the Sisyphus story: Karnus and the Boneriders enjoy their cruelty, but enjoying it does not make their lives meaningful. Wolf's objectivism wins—a meaningful life is actively and lovingly engaged in projects of worth—which is exactly Darrow's living for more, contrasted with the Jackal's loveless, self-loathing pursuit of mattering.
- ch. 18 "III. To Live or Not to Live in the Society" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "9. Pierce’s Republic" **·** Plato — Allegory of the Cave; The Noble Lie; The Philosopher King; Justice in the Republic — Randall Jensen maps the Society onto Plato's Republic (Brown has said he drew on it): the Color hierarchy parallels the Myth of the Metals' gold, silver, and bronze souls, the Golds' scorn for Demokracy echoes Book VIII's account of degeneration into tyranny, and Leto's 'We are Plato's philosopher kings' claims a mantle Plato himself doubted anyone could ever fill. Darrow's story is the Allegory of the Cave run from below—a Helldiver literally raised in a mine, blinded by surface light, whose return to a shrunken, grayer garden mirrors the philosopher's homecoming—except Plato never imagined the prisoner carved into a Gold. The Noble Lie survives as the terraforming myth fed to lowReds while the surface has been habitable for centuries, and the chapter weighs Darrow's gospel ('we choose who we are') against Plato's caveats: you can choose who to be only within limits, if you are lucky and greatly helped.
- ch. 20 "10. Virtue Rising" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Aristotle on Friendship (philia); The Noble Lie — Darci Doll argues the Rising exposes the Society's intellectual oppression—each Color denied education and fed 'noble lies' about its role—and that lifting it sparks an 'Intellectual Reformation' proving Color does not dictate potential: Darrow out-performing Golds, Orion the un-carved Blue, Ragnar and Sefi exceeding their station. She uses Plato's Republic (producers, auxiliaries, guardians, the lower orders kept obedient by Noble Lies like the Reds' terraforming myth) as the Society's blueprint, then turns to Aristotle: potential is realized only through the right environment, instruction, and habituated character, and Darrow's practical wisdom—testing himself, reassessing after Titus and Cassius, doing what makes him his best self—lets him flourish and lead. Aristotle's critique of utility-only relations explains why the Society's alliances expire (Antonia executed once useless) while Darrow and Mustang's virtue friendships and just rule endure, opening a society where everyone, including women and lowColors denied opportunity rather than ability, can maximize potential.
- ch. 21 "11. Beautiful Colors and Unjust Societies" **·** Plato — Utopia and Dystopia; Justice in the Republic — Devon Brickhouse-Bryson asks whether the Society, plainly dystopian with respect to justice, might nonetheless be utopian with respect to beauty. Treating a society as an abstract object—a system of persons ordered into a community, not reducible to its members or its gravBoots and razors—and beauty as harmoniousness, the ordering of parts into a unified whole in the tradition of Aristotle, Aquinas, and Hutcheson, he shows the Color system straightforwardly instantiates that definition, each caste an organ of one well-functioning clock. But the harmony holds only if the castes are genuinely teleologically distinct; if that is mere Gold propaganda, the Society is not beautiful but a cacophony. Either way the chapter's real lesson stands against Plato: identifying justice with each part fulfilling its role conflates beauty with justice, and the Society shows how radically the two can come apart—possibly beautiful and radically unjust at once.
- ch. 22 "12. The Law of Red Rising" **·** Antonio Gramsci, Thomas Hobbes, Thomas Aquinas, John Locke, Jeremy Bentham — Cultural Hegemony; Natural Law; The State of Nature; The Social Contract — Christopher Ketcham frames the Society through jurisprudence's debate between natural and positive law, opening with Gramsci's hegemony: Reds have internalized the Golds' message that their slave toil is heroic terraforming service, becoming 'enabled martyrs' who hate rival clans rather than their rulers. He deploys Hobbes's state of nature versus state of laws (Reds live in a state of war against Mars while Golds legislate in a state of law), Locke's suggestion that a sovereign can leave some people in the state of nature, Aquinas-style higher law, and H.L.A. Hart's positivism with Bentham and Austin—a law need not be moral to be law—to argue the Golds' caste statutes are valid yet ungrounded. His coda casts Darrow as Homer Plessy: Goldness, like whiteness in Plessy v. Ferguson, is inheritable property Reds cannot claim, and because Reds who speak are hanged, the law excludes the very voices Hart himself said keep laws from becoming terrible.
- ch. 23 "IV. The Rising and Beyond" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "13. Mustang’s Future Generations" **·** Derek Parfit, John Rawls — The Veil of Ignorance; Justice as Fairness; Utilitarianism; The Difference Principle — Courtland Lewis asks what Mustang owes future generations when rebuilding the Society, first showing that standard moral theories stall: nonexistent people lack rationality, cannot contract, cannot be treated virtuously, and utilitarian forecasting fails since we cannot know whether the Jackal's nuking of Luna might have led, in the deep future, to prosperity. Derek Parfit's Reasons and Persons then strikes: any policy choice creates a different future generation, total utility drives the Repugnant Conclusion (a maximally populous world of barely-worth-living lives, uncomfortably like the Society's Reds), and average utility yields the mere addition paradox (Mustang's Society is both no worse off and worse off when Andromeda's low-pleasure civilization is added). The chapter's solution is Rawls: the original position behind the veil of ignorance—where the Sovereign would not know she is a Gold—yields justice as fairness and maximin reasoning for the just savings problem, choosing to save more than is consumed; against Tim Mulgan's objection that this loops back to the Repugnant Conclusion, Lewis answers that real carrying capacities make the repugnant world impossible.
- ch. 25 "14. Guns Don’t Kill Colors—Colors Kill Colors" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Thomas Aquinas, Augustine of Hippo — Doctrine of Double Effect; The State of Nature; The Ethics of Political Violence — Robert Arp argues from Hobbes's right of nature—self-preservation as the first law found out by reason—that individuals, and by extension oppressed peoples, have a right to the means of lethal defense, so arming the lowColors of the Society is justified. He weighs pacifist counterpoints (Augustine on self-defense as inordinate self-love, the Buddhist first precept, Camus's refusal to kill) and answers with Aquinas's principle of double effect: Darrow destroying the flagship to save Luna, intending the good while foreseeing the deaths, is justified, as is killing in defense of innocent children the Institute rapes and eats. The Society then illustrates why disarmament enables tyranny—Hideyoshi's Sword Hunt, Stalin's weapons bans, the Golds' razor monopoly—so that when lowColors finally receive weapons in Morning Star they become the means by which the police state falls: guns equalize the weak against aggressors and the people against the state.
- ch. 26 "15. Death Begets Death" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant — Forgiveness; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Tripartite Soul; The Golden Mean — The Bocks trace Darrow's education out of vengeance: in Plato's tripartite soul the spirited part (anger) must obey reason, and Aristotle's virtue of mildness—anger at the right things, toward the right people, for the right length of time—is the golden mean between slavish and irascible that Darrow has not yet reached. Darrow learns the difference when he hands Titus over to Cassius's vendetta and admits 'That wasn't justice': retribution in Kant's lex talionis tradition must be dispassionate and proportional, while vengeance is past-oriented and insatiable, and Darrow's own bombing of the Ganymede docks shows how troubling even his 'justice' remains. Against Darrow's violent justice-in-love the chapter sets Martin Luther King Jr.'s agape and loving-forgiveness—Sevro hanging and then forgiving Cassius, Darrow forgiving Tactus, Mustang pulling her brother's legs for a merciful death—closing with King's warning that constructive ends can never justify destructive means, and Darrow's own admission that 'the war is not over.'
- ch. 27 "16. Can We All Get Along" **·** John Locke — Forgiveness; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Natural Rights — Courtland Lewis tackles transitional justice after atrocity: with the Rising won, what is to be done with millions of Golds complicit in slavery, rape, and torture? He tests Peter French's virtuous vengeance—punishment that fits the wrong, grounded in Locke's natural rights—and finds Darrow's destruction of Gold society fails it (disproportionate, unsober, punishing young Julian for his ancestors' crimes), then turns to Jessica Wolfendale's argument that declaring anyone unforgivable adopts the wrongdoer's own devaluing outlook, exactly as Darrow becomes what he despises. The working model is South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission—confession, conditional amnesty, truth-telling, reparations, Tutu, Mandela, Beth Savage hoping to meet her bomber—applied to Mars through Mustang-style dignified engagement on Adam Michnik's model and Slavenka Drakulic's lesson that every Color inherits responsibility for rejecting the Society's past.
- ch. 28 "Guide to the World of Red Rising" *(notes)*
- ch. 29 "Bibliographic Institute" *(notes)*
- ch. 30 "Howlers, Helldivers, and Peerless Scarred" *(notes)*
- ch. 31 "Colored Index" *(notes)*

- ch. 9 "Scientifically, Introductions Are an Idiot Thing" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates — The Meaning of Life; The Death of God; The Unexamined Life — The introduction frames the whole book through the Rick/Jerry opposition: Rick is a Nietzschean artist-creator who insists the world is objectively meaningless and Godless yet keeps choosing his family, while Jerry is the herd-animal chasing socially approved values. It claims the show, like Nietzsche's deliberately difficult writing, sorts its audience into Jerrys who enjoy the dick jokes and Ricks who do the hard philosophical work of finding microscopic meaning in a meaningless cosmos. It closes with Socrates's 'unexamined life is not worth living' to justify submitting to philosophy's perplexity even if the Eyehole Man kicks the shit out of you.
- ch. 10 "I So We Bailed on That Reality and We Came to This One" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "1. The Genuine Article" **·** Robert Nozick, Plato — The Experience Machine; Personal Identity; Truth as What Works — Written in the voice of a non-C-137 Rick, the chapter argues that whether the Beth at the end of 'The ABCs of Beth' is a clone doesn't matter, because our reverence for 'the genuine article' (like the original US Constitution) is romantic packaging, and a functional clone is as good as the original. It tests Robert Nozick's experience machine, whose three objections supposedly show we value genuine reality intrinsically, against Rick's pragmatism of believing what is useful, and reads 'The Wedding Squanchers' (Rick turning himself in to the Federation) as proof that his family is both instrumentally and intrinsically valuable to him. Your answer to the clone question, it concludes, is a Rorschach test revealing what you place intrinsic value on.
- ch. 12 "2. The Unimportance of Identity When You Have a Portal Gun" **·** Derek Parfit, John Locke — Teleporter Paradox (personal fission); Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory) — The chapter argues Rick C-137 is already dead: the Brainalyzer body-hops in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption' and the Operation Phoenix swap in 'Big Trouble in Little Sanchez' copy psychological states rather than transfer a consciousness, so each post-transfer Rick is a new psychological clone, exactly as in Parfit's Teletransporter. Building from Locke's memory theory of personal identity to Parfit's claim that identity is not what matters, it reads the dimension-hop in 'Rick Potion #9', the Morty voucher, and the ambiguous clone Beth of 'The Rickchurian Mortydate' as the show itself endorsing psychological continuity over numerical identity. What matters is that someone carries on Rick's desires and relationships, so nobody noticed the protagonist's death.
- ch. 13 "3. The M. Night Sh-imulation Hypothesis" **·** Nick Bostrom, Plato, René Descartes, William Paley — The Simulation Hypothesis; Allegory of the Cave; Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Philosophical Skepticism — The chapter runs Bostrom's simulation argument against 'M. Night Shaym-Aliens!', where the Zigerions trap Rick in simulations-within-simulations to steal his concentrated dark matter formula, and reads their cheap shortcuts ('My man!' NPCs, human music, Jerry's Appley award) as the glitches and shadow-people Bostrom predicts. It presses the epistemological problem that any evidence for the simulation equally supports its denial, an underdetermination that devastates the theory, and traces the lineage of 'the real world isn't real' through Plato's summoners and allegory of the cave, Descartes's dream doubt, and Paley's design analogy (Morty as the beautiful machine), ending with the microverse battery of 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy': this is the universe we live in, so get used to it.
- ch. 14 "4. Could a Divine Creator Turn Out to Be a Selfish Jerk" **·** William Paley, Alvin Plantinga, Plato, David Hume — The Watchmaker Argument (design); Euthyphro Dilemma; The Ontological Argument — Using 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy', where Morty discovers Rick's car battery is a microverse of gooble-box workers ('slavery with extra steps'), the chapter asks whether a universe's designer must be a perfect God or could be a clever jerk like Rick. It lays out Paley's watchmaker teleological argument, Hume's point that even a real designer need not be morally perfect, the Euthyphro dilemma against Divine Command Theory (would Rick's commands for middle-finger greetings become morally good?), and Plantinga's modal ontological argument recast across the show's multiverse of possible worlds like the one where Hitler cured cancer. It concludes that Rick's advice to just not think about it is exactly what Socrates refused to do.
- ch. 15 "5. Who’d Rick Kill Or, Who Killed Rick" **·** David Lewis, Gottfried Leibniz — Possible Worlds; Personal Identity — Framing Rick's massacre of the Council of Ricks in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption' as a crime-scene investigation, the chapter asks whether killing qualitatively identical Ricks is murder or suicide. It contrasts Leibniz's abstractionism (possible worlds as mere descriptions, pictured as the Palace of Fates in the Theodicy, allowing transworld identity via essential properties) with David Lewis's concretism/modal realism (all worlds really exist but are causally isolated, with world-bound individuals and counterpart theory instead of transworld identity). The show, it argues, is a modified concretism: portals let people interact across worlds, so Rick C-137 murdered distinct cosmic doppelgangers, not himself, as the interdimensional cable channels of 'Rixty Minutes' confirm.
- ch. 16 "6. Truth in a Multiverse" **·** David Lewis — Possible Worlds — Expanding outward from Rick's garage to define a 'world' as everything spatiotemporally connected, the chapter explains truth via the correspondence theory (claims are true when they match actual events, like the 2016 election) and the coherence theory (for truths like googol arithmetic that correspond to nothing). It argues that in Rick and Morty's world possible worlds are not abstract tools but real alternate timelines: Beth really could have been a human doctor and Jerry really could have been on DiCaprio's yacht, as 'Rixty Minutes' shows, and the Cronenberg timeline's brave Jerry proves a non-weenie Jerry is possible. Yet infinite timelines may still miss possibilities (Jerry's favorite even number), so abstract possible worlds keep a role, with David Lewis the lone real-world philosopher who took them as actually existing.
- ch. 17 "II Come Watch TV" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "7. Rick and Morty as Socratic Television" **·** Socrates, Plato — Socratic Method (elenchus); Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know); The Unexamined Life — The chapter argues Harmon and Roiland write the show as Socratic dialogue: in 'Mortynight Run' Morty's confident moral position (saving Fart from Krombopulos Michael is right) is dismantled until Morty himself pulls the trigger, leaving him in aporia; in 'Auto Erotic Assimilation' Summer's faith in freedom is razed by Unity's happy paternalist hive and the nipple-shaped race war it unleashes; and 'Look Who's Purging Now' refuses to choose between liberalism and conservatism when the post-purge town instantly re-founds the Festival. Like Socrates in Plato's Meno, the show's goal is not to teach lessons but to reduce viewers to confusion, because doing philosophy begins there.
- ch. 19 "8. Neither the Hero You Deserve Nor the Hero You Need" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Master and Slave Morality; The Übermensch; Will to Power; The Death of God — Reading 'Vindicators 3' through Nietzsche, the chapter argues the superhero team are slave-morality charlatans whose duty to protect the weak is the herd's imaginary revenge, while Rick, who defeated Worldender drunk, embodies master morality and honest will to power, against Jerry's dishonest version in the Pluto-not-a-planet fight of 'Something Ricked This Way Comes'. Rick's casual destruction of Worldender becomes Nietzsche's death of God, the collapse of the value-source that gave the Vindicators' lives meaning, which Vance Maximus denies at the cost of his life. The chapter then tests Rick against the Ubermensch via the camel-lion-child metaphor and concludes he is at best Nietzsche's lion, tainted by resentment over his lost family rather than the value-creating child, leaving Morty and Simple Rick as long-shot candidates.
- ch. 20 "9. The Fallacy of the Many Heads" **·** Philosophical Skepticism — The chapter uses Headism in 'Get Schwifty' as a case study in illusory correlation: Principal Vagina walks out to pray just as the Cromulons approve of Rick and Morty's song, so the town builds a false cause-and-effect religion from coincidence, compounding false positives until Beth and Jerry are nearly sacrificed to the Giant Heads. Drawing on Daniel Kahneman's System 1/System 2 model and Peter Wason's confirmation-bias studies, it argues the characters reason rationally on the information available but never check whether their information is sufficient, the same lazy thinking that sustains religious faith, ghost photos, and the Loch Ness Monster. The cure is effortful skepticism, stopping to ask whether we might be wrong, lest we end up shooting Mr. Poopybutthole.
- ch. 21 "10. On Being and Meeseeks" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Existence Precedes Essence; Bad Faith; Existentialism — The chapter asks what kind of being Mr. Meeseeks is and answers with Sartre: despite being 'created to serve a singular purpose', Meeseeks exhibit subjectivity, from the self-assertion of 'I'm Mr. Meeseeks!' to transcendence in envisioning Jerry's fixed golf swing and the anguish, forlornness, and despair of 'Meeseeks and Destroy' ('Your failures are your own, old man!'), so they must be beings-for-itself whose existence precedes essence, freely choosing accomplishment as their meaning. Along the way it glosses Sartre's facticity with Morty's hopeless crush on Jessica, essence-precedes-existence with the butter-passing robot, and bad faith with Jerry's assumed mediocrity and Beth's shrinking of herself into horse surgeon, wife, and mother until Mr. Meeseeks reminds her she is still an individual.
- ch. 22 "11. Are You Imagining That Poopybutthole" **·** René Descartes, Thomas Aquinas — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); The Cogito; Philosophical Skepticism — Reading 'Total Rickall' as an evil-genius scenario, the chapter treats the memory parasites (Uncle Steve, Sleepy Gary, Reverse Giraffe) as Descartes's deceiving demon lodged in the Smiths' reconstructive memories, with Rick's written headcount an empirical defense that methodical doubt undermines. Morty's formula that parasites implant only good memories is shown to be merely inductive rather than certain like the cogito, so Beth's shooting of Mr. Poopybutthole becomes the test case: applying Aquinas's three kinds of ignorance, the chapter argues she remains morally responsible despite genuine remorse because she neglected the chance to reconsider Morty's probabilistic rule. The upshot is Descartes's advice to restrain the will beyond what the intellect certifies: shoot for the arm, not the head.
- ch. 23 "III I Have No Code of Ethics, Just Love Killin’" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "12. Jerry’s Dick" **·** Peter Singer — Utilitarianism; The Drowning Child (obligation to aid) — Twin essays by two dimension-swapped Wayne Yuens debate whether Jerry owes Shrimply Pibbles his penis in 'Interdimensional Cable 2'. Yuen H-232 defends supererogation: like donating blood or a kidney to a Peter Singer figure, giving up the organ would be Good-Samaritan praiseworthy but beyond duty, since it would derail Jerry's life-plan and autonomy, and the artificial-heart alternative makes it optional, while utilitarianism has no room for such acts. Yuen U-964 replies that the life-plan excuse would absolve every shirked duty up to Evil Morty's massacre of the Citadel, that Singer-style obligation to aid stands, and that in our organ-short world we probably do have a duty to donate.
- ch. 25 "13. Rick, Morty, and the Cure for Unhappiness" **·** Epicurus — Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia); Death Is Nothing to Us; The Meaning of Life — The chapter diagnoses Rick's 'Wubba Lubba dub-dub' ('I am in great pain, please help me') as chronic Epicurean suffering and prescribes the tetrapharmakos, the four-part cure. Don't fear the gods: Epicurus's indifferent atomist gods versus Rick's atheism, his panic prayer in 'A Rickle in Time', and Toxic Rick's 'If god exists, it's me' as ego rather than argument. Don't fear death, since 'where death is, I am not', though infinite replacements make Rick and Morty fear each other's death rather than their own. The good is easy to get, so booze, Eyeholes, and Szechuan sauce must yield to water, friends, and family; and the terrible is easy to endure, as when Rick stops resenting Birdperson's wedding and finally turns himself in for his family.
- ch. 26 "14. Jerryboree!" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Immanuel Kant, René Descartes — Bad Faith; Respect for Persons — Arguing that even the interchangeable Jerrys of Jerryboree deserve better, the chapter uses Stephen Darwall's distinction between recognition and appraisal respect: Jerry lacks both, while Rick has appraisal self-respect (he loves his genius) but squanders recognition self-respect by portal-hopping away from every consequence. Jerry's spinelessness is then Sartrean bad faith, from celebrating being 'assigned a function' in 'The Wedding Squanchers' to needing the parasite Sleepy Gary to vouch for his very existence in 'Total Rickall' and lying to Keara in 'The ABCs of Beth'. The chapter closes with Thomas Hill's Kantian case that servility disrespects the moral law in oneself, quoting Kant's worm maxim against Jerry's failed him-or-me ultimatum in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption'.
- ch. 27 "15. Loving Your Pet Is Better than Utilitarianism" **·** David Hume, Peter Singer — Utilitarianism; Is–Ought Problem; Animal Liberation — Against Peter Singer's utilitarian case in Animal Liberation, spare Snuffles because he can suffer regardless of intelligence, the chapter argues utilitarianism fails because it quantifies the unquantifiable, happiness. It turns to Hume: intelligence cannot ground moral worth, since smart Rick enslaving a microverse would then be our moral superior; Hume's guillotine separates descriptive from moral claims so that metaphysics no longer decides who counts as a moral object; and Hume's real ground is sentiment, dogs loving across species as the tail-wagging Snuffles does. So the morally right response to 'Lawnmower Dog' is not Jerry's abuse or even Rick's intelligence helmet but simply loving the pet.
- ch. 28 "IV God, Grandpa, You’re Such a Dick!" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "16. He’s Ethickle Rick!!!" **·** Thomas Hobbes — The Social Contract; Ethical Egoism; The State of Nature — The chapter reads the Galactic Federation as Hobbes's Sovereign: Earth covenants in for security and gets an interplanetary TSA, pill-currency debt, and the surveillance droid Conroy, while the Citadel of Ricks tours Hobbes's three commonwealths in 'The Ricklantis Mixup', aristocratic Council, brief democracy, and Evil Morty's monarchy, where the Sovereign's rules cannot by definition be unjust. Against this, Rick embodies Hobbes's psychological egoism ('the object to every man is his own pleasure'), hiding his motives in the Riq IV hostage gambit and the Szechuan-sauce confession. Yet the chapter argues Rick's egoism is oddly ethical: in an infinite multiverse resources are not scarce, so refusing to surrender freedom to any Sovereign and competing for everything is the right way to live, with 'A Rickle in Time' and the self-sacrifice of 'The Wedding Squanchers' as its tested limits.
- ch. 30 "17. Who Is “Rick” Anyway" **·** Saul Kripke, David Lewis — Naming and Necessity (rigid designators); Possible Worlds — Starting from the mangled sentence 'Rick is the Rickest Rick who ever Ricked', the chapter asks what the name 'Rick' refers to in a multiverse. It contrasts Saul Kripke's view, names rigidly designate the same person across imagined counterfactuals, which would absurdly make the Council of Ricks one many-located Rick, with David Lewis's counterpart theory, each possibility a real world of world-bound duplicates. The show sides with Lewis: the Council says 'Rick C-137', C-137 works like a distinguishing last name, and Morty's 'I eat breakfast twenty yards away from my own rotting corpse' in 'Rixty Minutes' is true only because the corpse belongs to a Morty just like him. The chapter ends by noting Lewis never handled inter-reality travel, so which Summer C-137 Morty now refers to remains open.
- ch. 31 "18. What Makes Rick Tick" **·** Ethical Egoism; Anarchism — Surveying Rick's values area by area, a many-worlds multiverse, atheism ('There is no God, Summer'), scientism, egoistic ethics, hatred of all government, and rap as today's Romanticism, the chapter rejects absurdism, existentialism, nihilism, and even Max Stirner's individualist anarchism, which it says fits the Citadel of Ricks rather than the loner Rick. Its thesis is that Rick is an Ayn Rand Objectivist: Rand's ideal man of reason, independence, and rejection of altruism, collectivism, and mysticism, with Jerry as the pity-parasite anti-ideal exposed in 'The Whirly Dirly Conspiracy'. It warns that infinite choice risks the paradox of hedonism, pointing to Rick's half-hearted suicide machine after Unity, and ends that only chosen constructive goals, perhaps a kinder Rick, could save him, if some other universe didn't already have that Rick.
- ch. 32 "19. The Citadel of Ricks Is Untruth" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Socrates — Authenticity; Socratic Method (elenchus) — The chapter reads Rick C-137's war on the Citadel through Kierkegaard's claim that the crowd is untruth: the Council of Ricks is the leveling public, envying and punishing the passionate individual ('You're a rogue Rick, irrational, passionate'), as Rick J-22's breakdown over Simple Rick's wafers in 'The Ricklantis Mixup' dramatizes, while our Rick stays himself by refusing consensus. From Philosophical Fragments, via Socrates's maieutic midwifery, it draws Kierkegaard's ethics of selfhood: one person can only be the occasion for another's self-knowledge and must then push them away to become individuals. That is exactly Rick's advice to Beth in 'The ABCs of Beth', to leave Jerry, saddle her universe, and become herself, since only Beth can make Beth.
- ch. 33 "20. Getting Your Shit Together Stoic Style" **·** Epictetus — The Dichotomy of Control; Stoicism; The Unexamined Life — The chapter argues Rick is at his best an Epictetus-style Stoic: in 'A Rickle in Time' his total certainty keeps the split timelines perfectly synced, enacting 'choice alone is vice, choice alone is virtue'; his 'love is a chemical reaction... focus on science' speech in 'Rick Potion #9' treats passion as an impression outside the sphere of control; and his 'don't think about it' dismissal of the Hitler-cured-cancer reality applies the dichotomy of control to an unmasterable multiverse. Epictetus's model of hardship as training is vindicated by Cronenberged Jerry, whose struggle preserves his dignity in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption', and the chapter closes with the Stoic promise Rick's life shows: not pleasure but contentment.

## Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Rush and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Listen to My Music, and Hear What It Can Do" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction frames Rush as a 'thinking man's band': a cult favorite deliberately outside the mainstream whose fusion of virtuosic, structurally complex music with lyrics on social, scientific, and historical themes triggers both fierce devotion and passionate hatred in listeners. It sketches the band's history from its 1968 Toronto cover-band beginnings through Neil Peart's 1974 arrival and the album-oriented-rock success of Moving Pictures ('Tom Sawyer', 'Limelight'), arguing that Rush's lasting achievements come when thoughtful lyrics and progressive/hard music work together. It invites readers to treat each essay as one voice in an ongoing dialogue and to accept that being different, like Rush, is not a bad thing.
- ch. 6 "PART I - To the Margin of Error" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Houston, We Have a Problem, or, What Goes Up Must Come Down" *(no index entry yet)* — Auxier interleaves a memoir of sneaking off to Rush's 1977 Memphis concert (the Halloween-weekend ruse with his friend Brice, beers at J-Wags Lounge, the first hangover, and the setlist from 'Bastille Day' through '2112') with a philosophical defense of the band. He rejects the charge that Rush is a vehicle for Ayn Rand's objectivism, arguing Rand was a novelist with 'philosophical moments' whose analogy-built system is not philosophy, and that Peart quickly outgrew her influence by Moving Pictures. Working from Susanne Langer, he claims Rush assimilates lyrics to music (so 'Tom Sawyer' and 'Limelight' need no poetic standard), that music is a 'virtualization' of time creating the illusion of felt life, and that Rush's live processed sounds are second-order virtualizations whose only real test is whether the music is good.
- ch. 8 "Coda" **·** Cultural Hegemony — Bowman surveys the fifty-four recorded Rush tributes of 1996-2005, from the Barenaked Ladies quoting the 'Tom Sawyer' swagger riff in 'Grade 9' to DJ Z-Trip's trip-hop remix, Disarray's death-metal version, Deadsy's industrial take, and string-quartet translations, arguing that Rush's ambiguous genre coding is what lets this 'musicians' music' travel across mutually exclusive fan communities. He builds his own 'scholarly meta-remix' interleaving six versions of 'Tom Sawyer' in different keys and meters, and reads the 7/4 instrumental section's fate in each cover. Borrowing Robert Walser's claim that musical meanings are grounded in an ideological field where institutions enforce preferred meanings, he concludes that tribute artists find 'refractive, distorted, and disruptive' meanings in Rush, and that progressive rock served as 'substitute classical music' for working- and lower-middle-class fans.
- ch. 9 "The Heart and Mind United" **·** The Dialectic — Sheinbaum argues against the assumption that Rush's rhythmic complexity is 'thinking' music opposed to bodily groove, showing through close listening that 'Subdivisions' (7/8 in 2+2+3 groups), 'Limelight' (4/4 and 3/4 bars interleaved), 'Jacob's Ladder' (alternating 5/4 and 6/4), and the 7/8 passages of 'La Villa Strangiato' all groove while the band retains standard eight-bar phrase structures. He treats meter and hypermeter as Western cultural constructions, and reads Rush's metric deviations as a musical image of the individual resisting a 'conformist social order' (citing Chris McDonald on the individualism Rush shares with Ayn Rand's middle-class virtues). His resolution is dialectical: complex and conventional elements operate as simultaneous poles in synthesis, so mind and body, thought and groove, are united rather than opposed, a point he presses against the racialized mind-body binary in writing about rhythm.
- ch. 10 "No Heart to Lie" **·** Authenticity — Reuland uses YouTube drum covers of 'The Body Electric', 'Subdivisions', and 'YYZ' to analyze Rush's 'aesthetic of replicability': songs built as artifacts meant to be reproduced note-for-note, signaled by literal codes like the Morse-code intro to 'YYZ' and the binary '1001001' the android of 'The Body Electric' must crack to become human. He explains why critics deride this anti-expressive virtuosity by way of Amiri Baraka's racial coding of technique, Pierre Bourdieu's account of how 'natural' taste is legitimated while studied learning bears class stigma, and Mary Bucholtz's picture of nerds as hyper-white; the fans' literal meritocracy parodies the information economy's promise that skill converts directly into success. Finally he reads 'Limelight' as Rush's skepticism toward performance as a 'gilded cage' of inauthenticity, so that play-along videos recode performance as self-improvement that cannot be faked.
- ch. 11 "He’s Got to Make His Own Mistakes" **·** Plato, Walter Benjamin, Aristotle — Allegory of the Cave; Theory of Forms — Cole pits Plato against Walter Benjamin to vindicate the imitation of Rush: Plato's cave makes art a shadow twice removed from the Forms, and on that view a perfect copy is impossible and every cover degraded, while Peart's 'Limelight' calls the stage a 'gilded cage' that is 'just a prettified cave' yet, with 'we are merely players' (via Shakespeare), makes performing the way out rather than deeper in. Benjamin's translator essay, with its 'language forest' echo and 'pure language', shows how Rush's cover of 'Summertime Blues' on Feedback layers Blue Cheer and the Who into one perception, and how live variations of 'Witch Hunt' and the premature chord of 'Turn the Page' let error overtake and become the new original. The chapter exceeds Aristotle's principle of non-contradiction in 'pure language', where original, copy, and fan covers (Rock Band failures, the South Park 'Lil' Rush' flub, Rick Mercer's drum lesson) are fragments of one greater vessel, so errors are portals of discovery.
- ch. 12 "PART II - The Ebb and Flow of Tidal Fortune" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "Enjoy These Moments" **·** Epictetus — The Dichotomy of Control; Living in the Present — Earleywine argues that Rush's lyrics trained a generation in the core moves of cognitive-behavioral therapy, an idea he traces back to Epictetus before Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck rediscovered it against Freudian orthodoxy. He maps specific distortions onto specific songs: 'Witch Hunt' on dichotomous labeling, 'Distant Early Warning' ('black and whites of youth') on all-or-nothing thinking, 'Emotion Detector' on emotional reasoning, 'Vital Signs' and 'Totem' on thoughts altering perception, and 'Subdivisions' ('Conform or be cast out') as realistic critique rather than maladaptive thought. The final step, acting on examined values and savoring the present ('Time Stand Still', 'The Camera Eye', 'Chain Lightning'), makes the songs the incarnation of their own advice: just listen.
- ch. 14 "Smashing Critics’ Pumpkins" **·** Plato — Theory of Forms — Reisch reconstructs the rock-critical case against Rush ('pretentious', 'ridiculous', Greg Kot's jibe that Peart drums 'like he's working out a calculus formula') as resting on an implicit Platonism: the Forms fix what a 'real' rock'n'roll band is, so a band mixing rock with philosophy, literature, and mathematical precision seems to violate the metaphysical grain of the universe rather than merely disappoint a taste. He explains the Forms through Plato's trees and the Form of the song ('La Villa Strangiato' and 'Happy Birthday'), reads Jack Black's 'one atom' praise of Peart as mathematics-as-highest-knowledge, and treats the 'Aristocrats' joke and UFO mocking Geddy Lee as incongruity humor at kinds illicitly combined. Dropping the Platonic metaphysics of kinds collapses the critics' syllogism into a bare insistence that different is bad, which is the revenge Gene Simmons ('What kind of band is Rush? It's Rush.') and Billy Corgan ('they just don't fit in a neat box') already delivered.
- ch. 15 "Let Your Heart Be the Anchor and the Beat of Your Own Song" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Henry David Thoreau — Existence Precedes Essence; Radical Freedom and Responsibility; Walden (deliberate living) — Berti reads Neil Peart's 1997-98 catastrophes (his daughter's car accident, his wife's cancer death) and the 55,000-mile Ghost Rider motorcycle exile through Sartrean existentialism: existence precedes essence, so with no God-given script Peart must author his own reactions, exactly as Sartre's student had to choose between mother and Resistance. The chapter tracks alienation ('I do not know who I am'), the duty to choose rather than lean on outside voices, and 'The Pass' as the voice telling a suicidal teenager to walk back from the razor's edge. Thoreau's Walden retreat supplies the model for the healing road, and Peart's own directives ('keep moving; kick your own ass, gently') enact 'Freewill' and 'Something for Nothing': we are the ones who choose, and the choice to live made all that followed (re-marriage, Vapor Trails, five more tours) possible.
- ch. 16 "Hope" **·** Lucretius, Epicurus — On the Nature of Things; Atomism; Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia); Faith and Reason — Beck reads Snakes & Arrows as popular Epicureanism delivered by Lucretius' method: just as De Rerum Natura puts honey on the rim of the cup so Romans swallow philosophical medicine disguised as poetry, Rush's melodies smuggle reflection on pain, luck, and religion past listeners who think they are just rocking, with repeated choruses doing the work of Epicurean prolepsis. The random swerve of atoms explains 'The Larger Bowl''s unequal fortunes ('Some are blessed and some are cursed'), while the shore-watcher's relief at another's shipwreck and the concertgoer's pleasure exemplify Epicurean ataraxia. 'Faithless' and 'Armor and Sword' ('Pray and pass the ammunition') echo Lucretius' trampling of superstitious religio, and the chapter closes with Philodemus' Herculaneum scroll: don't fear god, don't worry about death.
- ch. 17 "Tallying the Total" **·** Jacques Derrida — Deconstruction — Kreuger applies Derrida's 'Differance' to how Rush gets valued: Hugh Syme's starman, pentagram, and bunnies are signs whose meaning defers down a chain, so no description of Geddy Lee ever touches the thing itself, and the band's twenty-four gold albums (economic value) never settle the contested question of cultural value that critics deny and fans affirm. Time defers value too: 'Time Stand Still' and the concert ticket sell a moment already gone, bootlegs and leaks chase the unrepeatable experience, and radio distance once hid songs like '2112' from value. 'The Spirit of Radio' carries the thesis in its own lyric, 'bearing a gift beyond price, almost free', where 'the words of the profits' on the studio walls measure sold value against integrity, and deferral finally emerges as Derrida's 'condition of possibility' that lets Rush's cultural value recover through Colbert, Rock Band, and I Love You, Man.
- ch. 18 "Sweet Miracles of (Secular) Faith, Hope, and Love" **·** Aristotle, Albert Camus, Socrates, Jean-Paul Sartre — Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing); The Absurd; Faith and Reason — Florek reconstructs Peart's ethics as Aristotelian virtue ethics: aiming at eudaimonia rather than feeling good, 'Freewill' chooses autonomy and responsibility as virtues, and 'Vital Signs' adds persistence and courage ('courageous convictions will drag the dream into existence'), with a compassionate expansion toward ordinary sufferers in 'Distant Early Warning', 'Red Sector A' ('I must help my mother stand up straight'), and 'Everyday Glory'. Peart's existential consciousness then confronts finitude ('Time Stand Still', the fading memory of 'Vapor Trail'), contingency ('Roll the Bones' — 'Why does it happen? Because it happens'), and the absurd of Sartre and Camus ('The Stars Look Down' — an indifferent universe that answers nothing). The 1997-98 tragedies turn this existential consciousness tragic, and the post-tragic resolution of Vapor Trails and 'Faithless' is a secular faith in hope and love — Peart's answer to 1 Corinthians 13 without God — grounded in being loved by Carrie Nuttall.
- ch. 19 "PART III - I Want to Look Around Me Now" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 20 "A Single, Perfect Sphere" **·** David Chalmers, René Descartes — The Hard Problem of Consciousness; Mind–Body Dualism; The Apollonian and the Dionysian — Reads Rush's 'Hemispheres' as a correction to Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness: Apollo's gifts of reason leave the people joyless, Dionysus's release into passion leaves them starving in winter, and Cygnus is made god of Balance because human nature thinks and feels at once. Against Descartes's two substances and the 'Robots Plus' picture, the author argues feeling is not supernatural icing on a machine but how survival-minded organisms stay in phenomenal contact with the world, so physicalism needs deepening rather than a nonphysical mind.
- ch. 21 "“I Want to Look Around Me Now”" **·** Simone de Beauvoir — Feminism — Charts Rush's gradual saturation with synthesizers, sequencers, and electronic percussion from 'Subdivisions' and 'Distant Early Warning' to 'Time Stand Still,' explaining the adoption through Wajcman's gradual-modification model and feminist analyses of technology as a male skill domain — including de Beauvoir's point that technical prowess underwrites virility, which the author applies to Rush fans' valorizing of the trio's chops. It closes by casting the band's handling of music technology as Bourdieu's habitus, granting Rush 'relative autonomy' from the hi-tech pressures of the 1980s.
- ch. 22 "Listen to My Music, and Hear What It Can Do" *(no index entry yet)* — A music-theoretic account of how Rush's music signifies only for competent listeners: the vocal pauses of 'Entre Nous' paint separation while its related keys paint unity, the 'Oriental riff' and pentatonics of 'A Passage to Bangkok' and 'Tai Shan' evoke nonspecific otherness, space-music textures open '2112' and 'Cygnus X-1,' and tritones brand evil in 'Witch Hunt,' 'The Necromancer,' and 'YYZ.' It ends by noting the irony that Rush uses its own electric voice to portray the bad guys, concluding with 'Entre Nous' that otherness and difference can be synthesized into a greater whole.
- ch. 23 "Does Rush Offer a Way Out" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, René Descartes — The Private Language Argument; Language Games; Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Brain in a Vat — Uses Rush's 1980s lyrics about facades and trust — 'Limelight''s strangers, 'Show Don't Tell''s refusal to take things on faith, 'War Paint''s lying mirror, and the synthesizer as an instrument that can fake any other sound — to stage skepticism about other minds, running from Descartes's cogito through solipsism and behaviorism. Wittgenstein's beetle-in-a-box and private-language argument dissolve the inner/outer confusion as a grammatical one, and 'Turn the Page' supplies the way out of the fly-bottle: nothing survives a vacuum, and with other people all we can do is be reminded.
- ch. 24 "Counterparts Lee’s Voice and Peart’s Drums" **·** Walter Benjamin — Takes the rock critics' vilification of Geddy Lee's 'shrill' voice versus fans' devotion to Neil Peart's drumming and explains the fan's pleasure through Roland Barthes's 'cruising': the listener repeatedly works through 'Tom Sawyer,' 'Between the Wheels,' and 'Animate' for the fresh catch of Peart's fills, which act as the Benjamin-style distraction by which the distracted mass absorbs the work of art. Lee's voice thus becomes an integral counterpart — the mundane the listener cruises past to reach the hooks that reward the quest.
- ch. 25 "PART IV - The Blacksmith and the Artist" *(front)*
- ch. 26 "Straining the Limits of Machine and Man" **·** Martin Heidegger, Karl Marx, Aristotle — The Question Concerning Technology; Alienation — Reads Peart's ambivalence about technology through Heidegger's techne as revealing and Marx's account of the worker: 'Working Man''s no-time-for-living day, '2112''s priests whose 'great computers' smash the protagonist's guitar, 'Manhattan Project''s Oppenheimer problem, and 'Test for Echo''s 'video vertigo.' Against Ellul-style autonomous technology the chapter insists Peart believes we still control our machines, and it ends with Rush mastering its own studio gear — and the motorcycle of Ghost Rider as the machine that carries Peart through grief.
- ch. 27 "Humanism Needs Its Evangelists, Too" **·** Baruch Spinoza — Faith and Reason; Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura); Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Treats Snakes & Arrows ('Far Cry,' 'Armor and Sword,' 'Faithless') as secular humanism stung by resurgent fundamentalism, and reads Peart's revolutionary trilogy — 'Beneath, Between and Behind,' 'Bastille Day,' 'A Farewell to Kings' — as Enlightenment humanism already anxious about its own decline. The core argument is rhetorical: Rush deliberately clothes humanist content in sacred and mystical language ('Something for Nothing''s Lord's Prayer motif, 'Jacob's Ladder''s storm read through Spinoza's God-as-nature and the experience of the sublime) because humanism needs evangelists who inspire wonder rather than mere argument.
- ch. 28 "There’s Something Here that’s as Strong as Life" **·** Robert Nozick, John Stuart Mill, Adam Smith — Ethical Egoism; The Minimal State; On Liberty — Argues Rush's lyrics cohere as libertarianism: Rand's rational self-interest in 'Anthem' and 'Something for Nothing,' Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain argument and Hayek's knowledge problem behind '2112' and 'The Trees,' Mill's 'experiments in living' in 'Witch Hunt' and 'Nobody's Hero,' and market-enabled tolerance and cosmopolitanism in 'Heresy,' 'Territories,' and 'Tai Shan.' Like Cygnus resolving Apollo and Dionysus, libertarianism takes the best of left and right, with individualism the constant running through Peart's career.
- ch. 29 "Hardly Rand-y Peart" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, G.W.F. Hegel — Utopia and Dystopia — Sets '2112' against Rand's Anthem to vindicate Peart's claim to be 'no one's disciple': both are egalitarian dystopias, but where Rand's Equality 7-2521 is a born transgressor who escapes to rebuild civilization, Rush's nameless protagonist is an indoctrinated conformist whose smashed guitar leaves him in Hegel's 'unhappy consciousness' and despair. Read as a romance of social disillusionment tinged with Nietzsche's joyful wisdom and gift-giving virtue, the song treats egalitarian leveling as nihilism and overturns Anthem's optimistic egoism — so it is hardly Rand-y at all.
- ch. 30 "Outro" **·** Cultural Hegemony — Asks how Rush is Canadian: CanCon radio quotas, the band's hybrid of British prog and Anglo-American hard rock, and McLuhan's 'flexible' national character, before a detailed musical reading of 'The Trees' — its 6/8-to-4/4 shifts, countertenor outburst, and woodpecker solos — as an aural 'Royal Commission' that may satirize legislated equality like Canadian content regulations defending against US media dominance. Bakhtin's monologic worldview frames the Oaks, and the chapter closes with later Canadian signs from the inukshuk cover of Test for Echo to Trailer Park Boys.

## Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "i" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "ii" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Reality of Scott Adams" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction sets up the book: in 2016 Scott Adams, a left-leaning Mensa member trained in hypnosis, predicted a 98-percent Trump landslide on the ground that Trump is a rare Master Persuader whose outrageous statements were calibrated weapons-grade persuasion aimed at irrational, emotion-driven voters who rationalize after the fact, and that the victory would rip a hole in the fabric of reality, producing cognitive dissonance and mass hysteria among Hillary supporters. It then profiles Adams's path from bank teller and 4 a.m. cartoonist at Pacific Bell to Dilbert creator, business guru (The Dilbert Principle and the Logitech gibberish mission-statement prank in a false mustache), fiction writer (God's Debris, The Religion War), talent-stack theorist of How to Fail at Almost Everything and Still Win Big, and author of Win Bigly, framing the volume as philosophy's examination of this gadfly.
- ch. 8 "I. In Front of Your Eyes" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "1. How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Tolerate the Master Persuader Hypothesis" **·** Socrates, Plato, Aristotle — Man Is the Measure (sophistic relativism) — Wolfe reads Adams's Master Persuader hypothesis through the ancient quarrel between Socrates and the Sophists: Derren Brown's deflation of hypnosis into one personality dominating another leads to Gorgias's Encomium of Helen, where persuasive words are magic spells that steal free will, and to Plato's Gorgias, where Socrates condemns rhetoric as cookery and cosmetics that flatter the ignorant while his disciple Polus covets its tyrannical power. On this mapping Trump's plain-talk style is simply Aristotle's available means of persuasion for a particular audience, and Adams is mostly a Sophist who treats words as programming code for moist robots, though he keeps a Socratic sliver in his stated aim of exposing readers to different ideas rather than converting them. Wolfe closes by refusing both readings of Adams as pro-Trump troll or alt-right hero, urging each side to see how persuasion actually worked on them.
- ch. 10 "2. Persuade Me Once, Shame on You . ." **·** David Hume, Plato, Immanuel Kant — Problem of Induction; Phenomena and Noumena; Philosophical Skepticism — Greene dismantles both phases of Adams's case that Trump is a Master Persuader. The trait-list phase (opening with big demands, the Intentional Wrongness Persuasion Play, never apologizing, exuding confidence, recruiting the reciprocity instinct, and the talent stack) fails because doing what master persuaders do is not being one, by the Tom Brady versus Archie Manning point that we never define good quarterbacks by wins alone and by the Kantian thought that an act must be done for the right reason. The reality phase borrows Plato, Hume, and Kant to deny us access to an objective world, but the chapter replies that the experts' predictive failures illustrate Hume's problem of induction rather than proving there are no facts, notes Adams even misreads Plato, and observes that nothing links the Persuasion Filter's one success to Trump's skills rather than to a one-off political climate.
- ch. 11 "3. How I Could Have Made Hillary President" *(no index entry yet)* — Taking Adams at his word that persuasion is learnable technique, Steele dissects Trump's linguistic kill shots (Low-energy Jeb, Crooked Hillary, Lyin' Ted, Pocahontas) as visual, confirmation-bias-proof forever names that killed Jeb Bush's candidacy in half a second, and contrasts the Clinton campaign's committee flops (Donald Duck, Dangerous Donald, Drumpf, and slogans like Love Trumps Hate and Stronger Together). He then practices what Adams preaches by drafting his own kill shot, The Don, a mafia frame built on offers that cannot be refused, omerta, and sleeping with the fishes, plus the slogan A Win-Win for America, engineered for positive repetition and the slightly-off meaning Adams calls intentional wrongness, concluding the election was winnable with commonsense marketing touches. An Orwell aside about whose victory a wartime poster really celebrates supplies the only classical rhetoric on display.
- ch. 12 "II. Comic-Strip Kafka" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "4. Scoundrels, the Lot of Us" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Søren Kierkegaard, Socrates — The Dialectic; The Stages on Life's Way; Socratic Method (elenchus); Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — Karavitis finds a Hegelian dialectic in the three-panel Dilbert strip (thesis, antithesis, synthesis) delivered through irony, then tests that irony against philosophy: Socrates' feigned-ignorance questioning that leaves interlocutors in aporia, Hegel's complaint that irony is vanity withdrawing from objective reality, and Kierkegaard's dissertation on the concept of irony plus Either/Or, where irony is the bridge from the aesthetic to the ethical life. The punchline is that after nearly three decades of Dilbert the white-collar workplace has not changed, so readers who feel superior to their bosses and co-workers have taken the vain, narcissistic, aesthetic reading Hegel warned against, making the joke a scoundrelly way of avoiding responsibility. A Leo Strauss aside casts Adams as an esoteric writer whose irony preserves him from the powerful.
- ch. 14 "5. The Serious Point of Scott’s Humor" **·** Aristotle, Socrates — The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics (arete); Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — Guerra and Barkman argue that Dilbert's humor is doing serious philosophical work: strips like the Pointy-Haired Boss's scheme to strip app users of free will, rebranded by Dilbert as marketing, distill manipulative corporate practice to its absurd essential core, and humor serves as a logical tool that, when it preserves the target's integrity rather than straw-manning it, exposes the equivocation in earnest arguments about getting something from nothing. They ground the practice in Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, where wittiness is the virtuous mean between the vices of buffoonery and boorishness, read Adams's catalogue of failures and his luck-first, passion-is-bullshit account of success as a Socratic acknowledgment of ignorance that deflates the American Dream, and treat Win Bigly's persuasion lessons (visuals, repetition, intentional mistakes, the Hitler counterexample) as further proof that Adams has the virtue of wit.
- ch. 15 "6. The PowerPoint Conspiracy Theory" **·** William of Ockham, Immanuel Kant — Ockham's Razor; Utilitarianism — In a sustained deadpan parody, Ketcham builds a conspiracy out of Ockham's Razor: William of Ockham's minimalist principle explains PowerPoint's big-type bullet points, but the slide deck (secretly engineered by DARPA with Microsoft, exported via Siberia to Putin) becomes a weapon that breeds stupidity, conditions Trump to tweet-length simplicities like fake news and crooked, and finally rigs him, not the voting machines. The chapter also wields the Razor correctly, insisting that a minimalist explanation must still be good and complete, as when little Jill's one bullet point tells us too little. Testing moral realism, Kant's absolute prohibition on lying, and utilitarianism's greatest happiness against the conspiracy's missing facts, it concludes we lack the information to render any moral verdict, which is exactly what the conspiracy-minded minimalists want.
- ch. 16 "III. It Tastes Better if We All Do It Together" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "7. Scott Adams’s Joy of Logic" **·** William of Ockham, Francis Bacon — Ockham's Razor — Bilsker turns Adams's Joy of Work catalogue of irrational co-workers into a critical-thinking syllabus: faulty analogy (from dogs fetching sticks to potatoes dancing, and Francis Bacon's body-politic passage praising war as exercise), huge-pants faulty causation, the Reinhart-Rogoff debt paper that drove austerity policy on mere correlation until Herndon, Ash, and Pollin exposed it, complex and objectionable cause, the overapplication of Occam's Razor to moon-landing hoaxes, misplaced authority, begging the question, and egocentric biases like I Am the World. He then contrasts the classroom view that confirmation bias is an unconscious background program with Win Bigly's claim that bias is the operating system itself, worrying about the implication that reasoning with anyone is futile, and concludes that Adams overstates how incapable we are of overcoming our biases.
- ch. 18 "8. Is It a Fact that Facts Don’t Matter" **·** Karl Popper, Aristotle — Falsificationism; The Web of Belief — Steele distinguishes facts as mind-independent reality from facts as expert-certified statements to show that Kellyanne Conway's alternative facts and Adams's own slogans trade on this ambiguity, and that Adams performatively contradicts himself every time he insists his predictions are true and matter. Analyzing the cognitive-dissonance hallucinations of Trump-is-Hitler and then Trump-is-incompetent, he argues that on Adams's own account brute facts proved irresistible, and that such belief revision is rational Popperian conjecture and refutation, plus the conservative strategy of saving fundamental theories (Coulomb's law) and dropping minor ones when the fuse blows. Against the claim that humans are irrational he recalls Aristotle's Rhetoric as persuasion's legitimate complement to the Prior Analytics, and leans on Percival to show propaganda fits a rational-reader model, citing the slow, fact-driven shift on gay marriage.
- ch. 19 "9. But Women Can Vote . ." **·** Simone de Beauvoir — Feminism; Objectification; Woman as the Other — Hansmann and Jones set Adams's gender posts against the four waves of feminism and the men's rights movement: his March 2011 Men's Rights post telling activists to get over it while lumping women with four-year-olds and the mentally handicapped, his Global Gender War matriarchy in which any country where women can vote counts as female-ruled, his framing of sex as a woman's currency for extracting male strategy (sacrifice a pawn to nail the queen), and his serial interrupting of women. They show the rhetoric eerily echoes anti-suffragists like Mrs. William Force Scott and Senator Sanford and the Goldilocks Dilemma, note the red-pill fantasy borrowed from The Matrix, and conclude that calling America a matriarchy defies scholarly consensus, with Beauvoir's The Second Sex marking why the vote never delivered the balance of power.
- ch. 20 "10. Intelligence and Duh-mocracy" **·** Plato, John Stuart Mill, Martha Nussbaum — Democracy; The Philosopher King — Saunders uses Adams's induhviduals and a hundred-voter dilution example in which smart people's votes are swamped to stage the classic case against democracy: Plato's physician analogy against Athenian rule by the ignorant and his philosopher-kings, Jason Brennan's hobbits, hooligans, and Vulcans with voter licensing, Mill's plural votes for the demonstrably wise, and Nussbaum's claim that humanities education breeds empathetic democratic citizens. Each fix fails on Dilbert's own terms, since competence tests demean the labeled, the Pointy-Haired Boss would amass extra votes while Dilbert-grade engineers lack political judgment, Asok's degree would not help, and the more educated are demographically skewed toward men. He concludes that equal votes win as a pragmatic default and muses that workplaces, not polities, might be the truer target of democratization.
- ch. 21 "IV. Comic-Strip Camus" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "11. Dilbert’s Absurd World" **·** Albert Camus, Jean-Paul Sartre, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Absurd; Rebellion and Revolt; The Myth of Sisyphus — Christian contrasts Camus's absurdity, the futile collision between our demand for meaning and a silent world whose only exits are suicide, a leap of faith, or Sisyphean revolt (an active defiance he takes partly from Nietzsche's rejection of resignation), with Adams's office absurdities. In Dilbert the absurd is contained and epistemic rather than pervasive and metaphysical: the battery-dead LED request, Dadaist mission statements, Catbert's evil HR policies, Wally's self-congratulatory Wally Reports, and Alice's harpoon all trace to people being idiots about different things, and could be fixed by honest credit and realizable plans. Dilbert's Business Dorky acceptance therefore looks Camusian but is not: it is recognition minus revolt, bewildered amusement where revolt and reform remain genuinely available.
- ch. 23 "12. Dilbert Is an Asshole and That’s Why He’ll Never Be Happy and Nobody Loves Him" **·** Aristotle, Jean-Paul Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Bad Faith; The Ethics of Ambiguity; The Golden Mean — Elsby and Luzecky argue Dilbert's unhappiness is chosen: from 400 rejections he concludes the women lack quality, he calls insult-bombing gentle kidding, and when Dogbert cites man's rational essence he chooses to watch all-star wrestling, each a textbook Sartrean bad faith where he glimpses the truth and flees it. Measured against Aristotle's eudaimonia he lacks every virtue of the Nicomachean mean (courage as the midpoint of fear, rightly scaled ambition, wit), and since one swallow does not make a summer his whole life, not a day of it, could earn the name happy. The December 2017 addictive-app strips complete the verdict: Dilbert monetizes a zombie-making app for a raise, making him Beauvoir's serious man from The Ethics of Ambiguity, the intelligent sell-out who subordinates human value to a hierarchy he knows is hollow.
- ch. 24 "13. The Essence of Dogbert" **·** Aristotle, David Lewis — Possible Worlds — Knuths asks whether Dogbert is essentially a dog and only accidentally white, importing Aristotle's Metaphysics distinction between essential and accidental properties and its modern modal gloss: essences are what an object has in all possible worlds, with David Lewis's concrete-constructionist reading noted against the standard view of worlds as abstract sets of propositions. The puzzle is that Dogbert's 2014 stint as CEO, combined with his canine essence, would prove dogs can be CEOs, threatening absurd conclusions about the real world unless we choose an ontology of fiction. Three candidates are weighed without a verdict: possibilism (Adams discovered a possible world), Meinongianism (Dogbert has being without existence, at the cost of square circles), and creationism (Dogbert is Adams's abstract artifact, troubled by the Not-Adams duplicate-creator case).
- ch. 25 "14. Of Course It Sucks—It’s Work" **·** Immanuel Kant, Karl Marx, Aristotle, Plato — Humanity as an End in Itself; Alienation; The Myth of Sisyphus; Respect for Persons — Wible stages three theories of work against Dilbert strips: the Greek view of Plato and Aristotle that labor is freedom-sapping and leisure is the civilized ideal, Marx's capitalist critique in which workers become objects and machines (Wally gives off no human vibe, and robots are coming for the engineers), and Desjardins's human-fulfillment model built on Schumacher's creativity, challenge, development, honesty, and beauty, with Wells Fargo's fake accounts showing how jobs that force lying corrupt character. He endorses instead a Kantian middle ground anchored in Norman Bowie's moral minimum: never treating workers as mere means, so the CEO making intern Asok drink industrial sludge on stage is a violation of respect for persons, not just bad management. Sisyphus supplies the image of pointless labor, though even he might be redeemed if he loved the rock.
- ch. 26 "V. Golden Age, Ready or Not" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "15. Bias Is Rational!" **·** Karl Popper — Falsificationism; Stoicism — Percival, whose Myth of the Closed Mind Adams cites, rebuts the Moist Robot Hypothesis that visual, emotional, repetitive anchors make us ninety-percent irrational. Against Kahneman's fast-and-dumb System 1 he sets Gigerenzer's ecological rationality (the gaze-angle heuristic that catches fly balls, the recognition heuristic that lets ignorant German students beat Americans on Detroit versus Milwaukee), then goes further with Popper's critical rationalism: babies as little scientists conjecturing and refuting, experience always theory-laden (the duck-rabbit), and Newton's boy on the seashore facing an infinite but navigable ocean of error elimination. The Stoic insight that all emotion is thoughtful and all thought emotional (the falling-tiles misperception that flips anger to relief) shows feelings track beliefs, so a free battle of the biases, not fact-free affirmation in the lineage of Le Bon and Pavlovian conditioning, is how rationality actually works.
- ch. 28 "16. Why Scott Adams Is Stupid" **·** Karl Popper, Paul Feyerabend, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Falsificationism; Anything Goes (epistemological anarchism) — Miori audits Adams's science talk through epistemology: warrant for belief, empiricism versus rationalism, Wittgenstein's demand for unambiguous clarity, and Clifford's epistemic responsibility, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence, which condemns sampling television news while blogging on climate science. Popper's falsifiability, learned from Einstein's willingness to be refuted against Freud's confirmation-seeking, exposes Adams's double standard in waving confirmation bias at critics while crediting his own predictions, and Feyerabend's epistemological anarchism is the view Adams most resembles, except that Feyerabend took responsibility and retracted. Cipolla's Basic Laws of Human Stupidity (the stupid person causes losses to both self and others) frames the closing charge: Adams suggests and retreats, sells product, and shirks the epistemic duty that experts in climate science and medicine shoulder.
- ch. 29 "17. Sweeping Up God’s Debris" **·** Socrates, René Descartes — Socratic Method (elenchus); Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Category Mistake; Philosophical Skepticism — Robison-Greene reads God's Debris as a Socratic dialogue on speed: the Avatar, like Socrates after the Delphic oracle, guts the Postman's confidence so he can unlearn, and the whole book functions as a Cartesian skeptical hypothesis in the dream-and-evil-demon lineage, here that we are the dust of a self-destructed God and perception is illusion, with gravity re-described as probability. Her counterattack is that the cosmology commits category mistakes, since probability cannot cause dust to reappear any more than Joe can consist of tallness, and that God made of probability is incoherent even for an omnipotent being. The five levels of awareness collapse too: level-four skeptics are just people who trust reliable methods, and the Avatar's claim that the mind is an illusion generator is self-defeating, since his own omniscience presupposes objective truth.
- ch. 30 "18. Scott Adams and the Pinocchio Fallacy" **·** Nick Bostrom, Karl Marx — The Simulation Hypothesis — Steele attacks Adams's embrace of the simulation hypothesis with the Pinocchio fallacy: a wooden boy cannot even hanker to be real, because hankering is conscious and wood is the wrong kind of stuff, and likewise no amount of code yields experience, since a simulation of weather wets no one and Deep Blue never knew it was playing chess. Bostrom's careful argument is distinguished from its popularizers, whose substrate-independence slide smuggles possibility into actuality (by the same logic a block of wood could be conscious), and the Matrix storyline, read as an allegory of Marx's exploitation and ideology, is judged as untenable as its energy-harvesting plot. Consciousness remains a property of living bodies, replication rather than simulation, and even if software minds were possible, trapping them in a fabricated world would be immoral.
