## Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Star Wars and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor William Irwin" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Heroes of Rogue Squadron" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "The Force Is with You . . . but You’re Not a Jedi Yet" **·** Plato, René Descartes, David Hume, Niccolò Machiavelli, Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre, Augustine of Hippo, Anselm of Canterbury — Euthyphro Dilemma; The Ontological Argument; Mind–Body Dualism; Problem of Induction — The editors' introduction argues that beneath its action scenes Star Wars stages ageless philosophical questions through the Skywalkers' struggles with identity, truth, freedom, and tragedy, opening with 'I've got a bad feeling about this' as basic philosophical wonder and doubt. It playfully transposes classic problems onto the saga: an Euthyphro-style question of whether Jedi virtues are good because the Jedi appreciate them, Anselm's question whether Yoda is a master greater than which cannot be conceived, Augustine on whether Anakin can be chaste 'but just not yet,' Machiavelli on Palpatine's Empire, Descartes' mind-body question asked of C-3PO, Hume's problem of induction applied to whether the sun will rise on Alderaan, Nietzsche's abyss for Vader, and Sartre's hell for the Sith. It previews each contributor's chapter rather than settling any question, framing the volume as a Kessel Run for the brain.
- ch. 8 "Part I - “May The Force Be with You”" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "“This One a Long Time Have I Watched”" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Thomas Aquinas, John Locke, Aristotle — Fate and Foreknowledge; The Divided Will; Free Will vs Determinism — Eberl argues that Anakin and Luke are radically free despite the Chosen One prophecy and Obi-Wan's 'you cannot escape your destiny.' Borrowing Augustine and Aquinas on God's eternity, he holds that foreknowledge (like the Jedi prophecy fulfilled when Vader destroys the Emperor) does not compel events - Anakin's choice makes the prophecy true, not vice versa - and applies Aristotle's tomorrow's-sea-battle to future-contingents like Obi-Wan's self-surrender on the Death Star. Using Locke's locked-room example and Augustine's account of 'inordinate desire,' he concludes that Anakin's fall stems from his own disordered will to control fate ('learn to stop people from dying'), while Han Solo embodies libertarian alternative possibilities ('No mystical energy field controls my destiny').
- ch. 10 "“Control, Control, You Must Learn Control”" **·** Epictetus, Seneca, Marcus Aurelius, Zeno of Citium — Stoicism; The Dichotomy of Control; Living in the Present; Stoic Cosmopolitanism (citizens of the world) — Stephens reads Yoda as a Stoic sage: Luke's first impressions are blinded by appearance, but Yoda exhibits the Stoic virtues of patience, timeliness, focus on the present, apatheia (freedom from fear, anger, and hate), and ascetic discipline (askesis), living by the dichotomy of control. He reconstructs the contrasting 'logic of the Dark Side' - anger to hatred to aggression to the mastery of others - showing the Emperor as a tyrant who, unlike the self-mastering Stoic (Marcus Aurelius being the counterexample among rulers), seeks to control what is not up to him, so Vader's 'I must obey my master' is servitude to vice. The chapter also marks Stoic limits: the Emperor rightly rejects felt compassion but wrongly refuses beneficence and Stoic cosmopolitanism, and Stoic physicalism cannot accommodate Yoda's 'luminous beings' afterlife.
- ch. 11 "“Great Warrior Wars Not Make One Great”" **·** Laozi, The Buddha — Taoism (Daoism); Zen Buddhism; Wu Wei (effortless action); Yin and Yang — Robinson (a Zen monk) argues the Force is best understood as ch'i and the Jedi path as philosophical Taoism and Zen: the Light and Dark Sides are the yin-yang polarity whose 'balance' Anakin's prophecy restores, and Anakin's fall is the Buddhist three poisons - clinging attachment to his mother and Padme breeding fear, anger, and hate. Yoda's teaching is Zen practice: 'You must unlearn what you have learned' is wu-wei (effortless action), 'Do or do not' rejects the divided mind of trying, and the Dagobah cave parallels the sword master Tesshu's koan insight that the real enemy is one's own mind ('no-enemy'). The chapter also traces Jedi genealogy to Bodhidharma's Shaolin kung-fu, the Korean Hwa Rang and Japanese Sohei warrior monks, and Bushido's samurai code, noting 'Jedi' derives from 'jidai geki'.
- ch. 12 "“You Know . . . What They’re Up Against”" **·** Thomas Hobbes, John Stuart Mill, Bernard Williams, Immanuel Kant, David Hume, Jeremy Bentham — Ethical Egoism; Utilitarianism; Integrity Against Utilitarianism; Humanity as an End in Itself — Dees finds moral ambiguity lurking in Star Wars' black-and-white universe: Han Solo's Hobbesian ethical egoism ('I take orders from just one person - me') is shown to be coherent and gradually transformed by friendship with Luke and Leia into commitment to a cause. Lando's betrayal of Han on Bespin is defended as a straightforward Mill-Bentham utilitarian choice by a responsible official, weighed against Bernard Williams's Jim-and-the-commandant integrity objection, which the author rejects as moral vanity. Count Dooku's apparent idealism is exposed as evil's tool, and Anakin's massacre of the Sand People is condemned as non-ambiguous barbarity via Kant's formula of humanity (and Hume on reason's role with the passions), leaving only late Vader as genuinely morally ambiguous.
- ch. 13 "Part II - “Try Not—Do or Do Not”" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "The Jedi Model" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Allegory of the Cave; The Golden Mean; The Noble Lie; Justice in the Republic — Barad presents a handbook of Jedi virtue modeled on Plato's Republic: the Jedi are Plato's Guardians, trained through physical exercise and Socratic questioning to guard peace and justice. Aristotle's golden mean explains courage as the balance between Chewbacca's cowardly fear and Anakin's rash rush at Dooku, with Luke's decision to leave Dagobah counting as courage because it has just cause. Luke's Dagobah cave vision (Vader's mask opening to reveal his own face) is read as Plato's Cave allegory turned inward - self-knowledge of one's fear of becoming evil - while compassion and forgiveness, not forbidden attachment, complete the Jedi character. The chapter even defends Jedi mind tricks via Plato's noble lie (the myth of the metals) as manipulation of the weak-minded for the common good.
- ch. 15 "The Fate of Evil after the Overthrow of the Empire" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Plato — The Problem of Evil; The Divided Will; Free Will vs Determinism — Brown treats Luke's 'Is the Dark Side stronger?' as the problem of evil: distinguishing natural evils (the wampa, bigger fish) from moral evils (Tarkin destroying Alderaan), he surveys the Platonic craftsman working recalcitrant matter and the Manichean dualism of two gods - the Emperor as would-be 'evil incarnate' - before giving Augustine's answer. On Augustine's free-will defense, no creature is inherently evil; the origin of each moral evil is the creature's own pride and free choice, so Anakin, not the Emperor's seduction, is responsible for his turn ('I'm a Jedi. I know I'm better than this'). The chapter ends on whether evil can ever be finally defeated, arguing the Jedi prophecies of 'balance' fit a world where evil is a permanent possibility that heroism needs.
- ch. 16 "Restoring Balance to the Force" **·** Peter Singer, Aldo Leopold — Speciesism; Anthropocentrism; The Land Ethic — Cooke uncovers an environmental ethic in Star Wars: after surveying anthropocentric resource-management views and Singer's anti-speciesism (Luke blithely shooting womprats, the Geonosian arena's abused beasts), she builds the chapter on Holmes Rolston III's claims that organisms and ecosystems have intrinsic value and that value is systemic and holistic. The 'living Force' - life creates it, midi-chlorians live symbiotically in all cells - makes Jedi training a discipline of respecting nature, exemplified by Yoda's mud hut on Dagobah and the self-sufficient Gungan and Ewok eco-communities that defeat droid armies and stormtroopers. Restoring balance to the Force therefore means restoring symbiotic balance between human culture and the natural world, which the chapter links to Leopold-style land-ethic holism of the biotic community.
- ch. 17 "Send in the Clones!" **·** Immanuel Kant, Plato — Just War Theory; Humanity as an End in Itself; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Hanley defends a provocative 'yes' to cloning, genetic engineering, and clone armies. He dismisses the 'yuck factor' as showing nothing inherently bad, argues via non-identity-style cases (a genetically corrected or maimed Luke is a different child who is not thereby harmed) that early genetic manipulation harms no one, and distinguishes brainwashing, coercion, and inducement (Obi-Wan's death-stick mind trick, Vader's threats to Lando, Jar Jar's exploitation) to ask when bending another's will is permissible. Turning to warfare, he applies Just War theory's conditions - judging Anakin's slaughter of the Sand People guilty on nearly every count - and concludes that troops with deliberately diminished autonomy may be the least objectionable solution to the ethics of recruitment, training, and deployment: send in the clones.
- ch. 18 "Part III - “Don’t Call Me a Mindless Philosopher!”" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Only a Jedi Can Save Us Forgetting and Recollecting" **·** Martin Heidegger, Parmenides, Heraclitus — The Question Concerning Technology; Dasein (being-there); Authenticity — Abrams reads the saga through Heidegger's philosophy of technology: the lightsaber Luke learns to feel as an extension of his body is the authentic 'ready-to-hand,' while the Death Star - a massive mechanical eye that enfames Alderaan on its viewscreen before destroying it - embodies the 'present-at-hand' gaze of enframing that converts nature into standing reserve (clone and droid armies, stormtrooper armor). Yoda on Dagobah is perfect attunement, an authentic being-in-the-world who is 'at home' with being, and the Force parallels Heidegger's being: everywhere, easily forgotten. Anakin's slide - slave of Watto, severed hand replaced by cybernetics, final encasement in Vader's armor - is progressive enframing and forgetting of his own being, and Luke's 'the name of your true self... you've only forgotten' is the recollection of being by which the Jedi, not a god, saves us.
- ch. 20 "It’s Not Our Lot in Life!" **·** The Turing Test; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Arp argues that C-3PO and R2-D2 satisfy the standard functional criteria of personhood - rationality, mental states, language, social relationships, and moral agency - opening with a blind listener who took Threepio's frightened chatter for a man, a Turing-test-style judgment from behavior alone. He catalogues evidence: Threepio's odds-calculating and Wookiee-winning deduction, Artoo's deceptive manipulation of Luke, the droid torture victim's screams at Jabba's palace, and the Chewbacca-Threepio quasi-familial bond on Cloud City. Since droids meet the conditions, their restraining bolts, cantina bans, and forced servitude are slavery, and the Galactic Senate should grant them limited rights - perhaps cheering a droid rebellion against the organic empire - a question the chapter urges on us as robotics approaches Moravec's predictions.
- ch. 21 "“May The Force Be with You”" **·** David Hume, Gottfried Leibniz, Bertrand Russell — Problem of Induction; Monadology; Philosophical Skepticism — Jones uses the Force's telekinesis (Luke's lightsaber flying to his hand, Yoda raising the X-wing) to probe the metaphysics of causation. Hume shows we never observe the necessary connection between cause and effect - only constant conjunction and habit - so Jedi mind-power is no more mysterious than gravity or magnetism; Leibniz's Monadology argues one substance cannot transfer properties to another, so 'how' any cause works is unintelligible; and Hume's problem of induction (will Tatooine's twin suns rise tomorrow? will Vader's officers always choke?) shows law-governed expectations cannot be non-circularly justified. Concurring with Russell that 'cause' is a relic, the chapter concludes the Force qualifies as a kind of cause precisely because our causal concept is too vague to exclude it - and plugs science fiction as a laboratory for sharpening concepts.
- ch. 22 "The Force of Love" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Plato, Epictetus, Thomas Hobbes — Geist (World Spirit); Platonic Love (the ladder of love); History Has a Direction — Lawler identifies Hegel's Absolute Spirit with the Force: Hegel's distillation of religious history - divine nature (the Ewoks worshipping C-3PO), the Roman Empire's transcendent Unhappy Consciousness, and Christianity's Consummate Religion - maps onto the saga's movement, with Anakin's virgin birth, prophecy, fall, and Calvary-like redemption fulfilling the pattern differently from the sinless Savior. The Dark Side is the separate ego asserting 'I' against 'We' (Hobbes's war of all against all culminating in the Emperor), and sin is the belief that one is an isolated individual. Against the Jedi's Stoic detachment (Epictetus), the chapter uses Diotima's ladder of love from Plato's Symposium and Hegel's Faust to argue that only passionate, attached love - Anakin's for Padme and Luke's for his father - descends into darkness and brings the Spirit's balance, so 'the Force is with us.'
- ch. 23 "Part IV - “There’s Always a Bigger Fish”" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "An Empire of Fear and Trembling" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Friedrich Nietzsche — Master–Slave Dialectic; Struggle for Recognition; Will to Power — Cameron reads the Emperor's dominion through Hegel's master-slave dialectic and struggle for recognition: fear is the Empire's currency, from Alderaan's destruction as visible demonstration ('fear will keep the local systems in line') to Vader's deliberately undefined threats ('The Emperor is not as forgiving as I am'), while hatred binds the Sith Master to Maul, Dooku, and Vader. Because the master can never win recognition from an unequal slave, Palpatine's will-to-power rule is a historical dead end, whereas the slave - Anakin laboring in Watto's shop, Luke overcoming his fear in the cave and under Yoda - can transform himself through work and courage. Vader's final turn is thus his achievement of a new self-consciousness, recognizing himself as 'something other than a slave' at the moment Luke's unshakeable faith forces the truth on him.
- ch. 25 "Palpatine’s Legacy" **·** Niccolò Machiavelli, Plato, Aristotle, John Dewey, Jean-Jacques Rousseau — The Ends Justify the Means; The Philosopher King; Democracy as a Way of Life; Democracy — Decker reconstructs Palpatine's career as a case study in how democracies die: using Aristotle's definition of tyranny and the precedent of Pisistratus and Julius Caesar, he shows Palpatine manufacturing the Separatist threat so the Senate grants him emergency powers - a twist on Machiavelli's loved-versus-feared dictum in which playing the reluctant democrat is itself the means to absolute rule. The Attack of the Clones debate between Anakin ('Someone wise' should make people agree) and Padme becomes a clash between Leo Strauss's philosopher-king ideal of rule by the virtuous few and John Dewey's conception of democracy as a way of life trusting the intelligence of common people, with Rousseau's social contract framing the stakes. The chapter concludes that democratic ends require democratic means and that unaccountable 'watchers' - Straussian statesmen or Anakins - are exactly the path to Empire.
- ch. 26 "“Luminous Beings Are We . . . Not This Crude Matter”" **·** Aristotle, Francis Bacon, Walter Benjamin — Aristotle on the Soul; The Four Causes; The Aura of the Artwork — Donnelly counter-reads The Empire Strikes Back against Aristotle's philosophical realism, in which nature is purposive, form and matter are inseparable, and each person is an irreplaceable primary substance. Lucas 'humanizes technology' - C-3PO reassembled like the Tin Woodsman, AT-ATs as beasts, Han slicing open the tauntaun with a sneer at its flesh, Luke admiring his new bionic hand - blurring Aristotle's art/nature distinction and reducing body to interchangeable machine parts, a Baconian will to power over nature that even Yoda's mind-over-matter training echoes (the chapter opens with Benjamin's remark that the copy eclipses the original). The result, he argues, is dehumanization: preferring the odorless tin heart to creaturely flesh trades the genuinely human for Gulliver's barn of horses.
- ch. 27 "“Trust Your Feelings”" **·** Plato, Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates, Immanuel Kant, The Buddha — The Noble Lie; Perspectivism; Utilitarianism — Fader tackles the paradox that Jedi lie while Sith tell the truth: Obi-Wan's 'Darth Vader betrayed and murdered your father,' Yoda's trickster masquerade on Dagobah, the Council's cover-up of its waning powers, against Vader's brutal truth at Cloud City and Palpatine's technically honest 'I love democracy.' Kant's absolute prohibition of lying is set against the utilitarian's greatest-good lie and Nietzsche's claim that truth is the accepted set of social lies; Obi-Wan's deception is then defended through Plato's noble lie and the Buddha's Parable of the House on Fire, where 'expedients' to save the oblivious are no falsehood, while Vader and Dooku wield literal truths as weapons without compassion. Luke's answer is to stop accepting anyone's version and build his own green lightsaber: truth as perspective, intention, and finally the heart's understanding that redeems Anakin.
- ch. 28 "“A New Hope”" **·** William James — The Will to Believe; Truth as What Works; Pragmatism — Long stages William Clifford's ethics of belief against William James's will to believe, with Luke Skywalker as James's exemplar. Clifford's shipowner story condemns faith as 'wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone,' which would convict Luke of immorality when he switches off his targeting computer and trusts the Force; James replies that where a choice is intellectually undecidable and a genuine option - live, forced, and momentous, like Luke's turn to the Jedi life or Obi-Wan's response to Leia's hologram - pragmatic faith is justified and even salvific. Faith can create truths: Han flying into the asteroid field, Luke's unjustified belief that there is good in Vader bringing Anakin back, the author's faith in his students, and Martin Luther King Jr.'s dream - all illustrating 'a new hope.'
- ch. 29 "Masters of the Jedi Council" *(notes)*

## Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Stephen Colbert and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Acknowledgements" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "Philosophy for Heroes" *(no index entry yet)* — Aaron Allen Schiller's introduction presents Colbert as a cultural institution (Time's 100 Most Influential, Emmy and Peabody awards, a 2008 presidential run) and a faux-pundit who does not report the news but 'feels the news at us' through the WØRD, Better Know a District, the ThreatDown, and the calls to action his fan army, the Colbert Nation, obeys. It argues philosophers love him because he 'tortures logic like Mozart writes symphonies,' playing with Truth and Reality through his coinages truthiness and wikiality so thoroughly that no future philosophical tract on the nature of Truth will be complete without considering truthiness. The book, it says, is for anyone who finds those concepts 'under their skin' without quite knowing why.
- ch. 8 "FIRST SEGMENT - The WØRD First Principles of Colbertian Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Where Do We Go from Here" **·** Socrates, John Locke — Moral Relativism; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — David Kyle Johnson argues that Colbert's gut-thinking persona (the Harriet Miers 'I know her heart' bit, 'that's my right' on the Panama Canal) satirizes a real and widespread vice, and he refutes the philosophies behind it. Individual and moral relativism collapse into self-contradiction and absurdity ('Lincoln was not assassinated' would be 'true for' someone; Hitler could not be condemned), while gut-justification is what Locke called 'enthusiasm' - a belief that is 'its own proof,' circular like the prophet whose revelation needs no burning bush. Following Jamie Whyte, he dismantles the 'right to my opinion' (running example: the friend who insists on a grassy-knoll shooter despite the melon-head evidence): there is no epistemic or moral right to undefended belief, and no right to intellectual comfort. Against this he holds up Socrates, wisest because he alone admitted ignorance, and insists philosophy and politics progress only through argument, so truthiness is never an acceptable substitute.
- ch. 10 "Explaining Moral Doubt" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Jeremy Bentham, John Locke, Nel Noddings, John Stuart Mill, Thomas Hobbes — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Categorical Imperative; Utilitarianism; Caring as the Ground of Ethics — Steven Gimbel reads the Formidable Opponent segment - red-tie Colbert debating blue-tie Colbert - as a glimpse of authentic moral deliberation that the flip-flop-phobic punditry satirized by the show (and Jon Stewart's Crossfire rant) has abandoned. Moral doubt is good because perspectives are partial and the Enlightenment 'marketplace of ideas' of Locke and Mill tests beliefs only through challenge. It has a source: 'morally right' bundles five dimensions - the actor's character shaped by habit (Aristotle's virtue ethics), the act itself judged by Kant's categorical imperative, the pleasure-versus-pain consequences tallied Bentham-style, the rights of the person affected from Locke and Hobbes's social contract, and the special care obligations of close relationships (Noddings and Ruddick) - and hard cases like abortion and flag burning are exactly where these dimensions pull apart. So emulate the dueling Colberts: fear not the flip-flop, since deciding which value trumps which requires open-minded conversation with oneself.
- ch. 11 "Under-Confidence in Reason Once It’s Easier Said, then It’s Done" **·** Socrates, Jacques Derrida — The Unexamined Life; Deconstruction — Roben Torosyan turns Colbert into a negative textbook for critical thinking: the character embodies the exact opposite of the American Philosophical Association's seven critical-thinking dispositions (inquisitive, open-minded, truthseeking, systematic, analytical, judicious, confident in reason), from refusing to imagine Lisa Randall's extra dimensions, to 'the market doesn't lie' about the Bible, to placing himself above Maimonides, Socrates, and Aquinas in the stem-cell Formidable Opponent. Each section names the fallacies his shtick commits - appeal to popularity, appeal to ignorance, composition, circular reasoning, wishful thinking, appeal to consequences - using real WØRD bits like the Iraq 'no casualties' monologue and the cake-metaphor exchange about the war. The WØRD's self-undermining bullet points are read as Derridean deconstruction (différance): every assertion shot through with what differs from and defers it. Watching Colbert fail at the examined life Socrates recommended, the viewer learns to catch such abuses in pundits and in themselves.
- ch. 12 "Sin, Play, and the “Synagogues of Satan”" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Heraclitus, Thomas Aquinas, Protagoras — Virtue Ethics (arete); Cardinal and Theological Virtues; Man Is the Measure (sophistic relativism) — Rachael Sotos argues the Report performs Platonic play: like the divine puppet of Plato's Laws with its competing cords, Colbert reveals what moves us (fear, hope, the ThreatDown bears, the 'golden cord' of the good) and so teaches freedom through play. Colbert's pompous self-authority - claiming to be 'the canon and measure' of virtue in I Am America - parodies Aristotle's serious man (spoudaios, megalopsychos) and the sophists Protagoras and Prodicus with their Orpheus voices, proving Heraclitus right that 'time is a child at play' and Aristotle wrong that play is mere medicinal rest. Tracking the war on fun from Chrysostom through Aquinas's eutrapelia (there is sin in a lack of play) to Erasmus's Praise of Folly and the Puritans' ban on theaters as 'Synagogues of Satan,' she reads Colbert's playing-at-sin - the man-seed eugenics bit, the 'black friend' boasts, the Ellen DeGeneres Paradox on Wikiality - as Erasmian folly that heals America's Puritan hangover in the culture wars.
- ch. 13 "Conclestions" **·** Bertrand Russell — Sense and Reference — Jason Southworth asks how viewers understand Colbert's deliberately confusing coinages ('wordanista,' 'superstantial,' 'Lincolnish,' 'freem,' and the title 'I Am America (And So Can You!)'). Borrowing Russell's view that names abbreviate definite descriptions (the 'spot check test'), he argues these utterances are paraphrasable and therefore meaningful rather than nonsense, distinguishing meaning from reference and literal from non-literal meaning. He then applies Grice's cooperative principle and conversational maxims to derive implicatures: the gut speech violates 'do not say what you believe to be false' and so implies truthiness-as-visceral-feeling, 'wordinista' imports Sandinista-style radicalism, and 'John, tear me a new one' generates the kitten-woodchipper joke. Since context fixes meaning, even dictionary-less words like 'freem' can be decoded, and the Wordinistas at Webster's are unnecessary.
- ch. 14 "SECOND SEGMENT - The ThreatDown Truthiness" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "Wishing and Dogmatism" **·** Harry Frankfurt — On Bullshit; The Will to Believe — Matthew Pierlott argues Colbert the satirist conflates two things his character, Stephen, merges: truthiness (trusting gut and heart over external authorities like dictionaries) and bullshit in Frankfurt's exact sense - speech indifferent to truth, which Pierlott finds in Hillary Clinton's dismissal of economists on the gas-tax holiday and likens to Steve Careill's habitual pleasantries versus Jon Stewart's honesty and Stephen's lies. He defends gut and heart as evidence-bearing tools - knowing a candidate's 'heart' from character evidence (the Westmoreland Ten Commandments interview), gut intuitions as unconsciously processed experience, and choosing which of the two Cheneys (1994 quagmire prophet or 2003 liberators booster) to trust - so in an information-saturated democracy truthiness is a necessary part of any orientation toward truth. The real enemy is dogmatism, the 'Dark Side of Truthiness' that cuts off future evidence, while wishful thinking kept modest (optimism that people are honest) can even be beneficial, a Jamesian willing-to-believe.
- ch. 16 "It-Getting The Truth about Truthiness" **·** Sextus Empiricus, David Hume, Michel de Montaigne, Nagarjuna, Pyrrho — Pyrrhonian Skepticism (suspension of judgment); Philosophical Skepticism; Man Is the Measure (sophistic relativism) — Ethan Mills runs a 'Better Know a Skeptic' four-parter applied to the show: Pyrrhonian skepticism (Sextus Empiricus's suspension of judgment and living by appearances, played out in the Jon-says-worst-versus-Stephen-says-greatest Bush debate), Modern skepticism (Montaigne's fideist custom-worship and Hume's dream argument for why knowledge of couches, Doritos, and presidents is impossible), and Indian skepticism (Nagarjuna's circle that means of knowledge cannot be established without things known, illustrated with Stephen Sr. and Stephen Jr. as both father and son, plus Jayarasi's destruction of epistemology). He adds 'political skepticism' - the American sense that political knowledge is impossible - which breeds wikiality, an internet relativism ('reality we just agreed on') that the WØRD's own bullet points ('Wikipedia can tell a lie') undermine. Truthiness, he concludes, is Stephen's false cure for political skepticism: commitment without facts, a 'truthiness of the appearances'; but Sextus shows skeptics can still act on appearances without dogmatism, so we can vote and argue on the best evidence, as in Sagan's science-as-democracy, without certainty.
- ch. 17 "But Does Political Satire Promote Democratic Values" **·** Michel Foucault, Herbert Marcuse — One-Dimensional Man — Michael Tiboris and Kory Schaff answer their title question affirmatively: Colbert's satire promotes democratic values by practicing Foucault's parrhesia - fearless speech that speaks the truth freely, functions as criticism of interlocutor and self, and flows from moral duty - unlike bumper-sticker assertion, since it enters risky dialogue and invites being refuted. Against this stands a corporate-consolidated media ('monopoly of meaning' from GE, Viacom, News Corp, Time-Warner) whose framing, slanting, and spinning - McCain's 'transcendental' war, the Obama-dresses-like-Ahmadinejad story, WMD as Word of the Year - exemplify Marcuse's one-dimensional thought absorbing oppositional language ('clean bomb,' 'harmless fall-out'). The WØRD models parrhesiastic critique by speaking media's own language while the bullet points undercut it ('Definitions will greet us as liberators'), exposing how politicians and pundits merely appear truthful and teaching viewers their own duty of critical assessment.
- ch. 18 "Philosophy in the Age of Truthiness" **·** Socrates — The Unexamined Life — David Detmer explains how the twentieth century's scientific persuasion techniques plus electronic media, American anti-elitism ('science is elitist... Gravity Without Representation'), the conflation of a legal right to an opinion with its being right, and journalism's bankrupt objectivity doctrine produced the age of truthiness that Colbert satirizes (Britannica and the Panama Canal, Limbaugh, O'Reilly, and Coulter as the 'gasbags'). He then rebuts the book's implicit challenge that philosophers' appeals to intuition are themselves truthiness: self-evident truths like 'cruelty is wrong' or Euclid's axioms are needed to stop the infinite regress of justification, and they differ in kind from gut-feelings about historical or political claims whose denial is easily conceived. The Report's nightly ridicule of truthiness therefore serves Socrates' dictum that the unexamined life is not worth living, showing philosophy's value to a public that lets pundits decide by gut.
- ch. 19 "THIRD SEGMENT - Better Know a Philosopher" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 20 "Colbert Is (the Tragedy and Comedy of) America, and So Are We" **·** Socrates, Plato — Socratic Method (elenchus); Allegory of the Cave; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know); The Myth of Sisyphus — Ralkowski asks whether Colbert is America's Socrates, comparing Colbert's ironic interviews (Caitlin Flanagan on feminism, Harvey Mansfield on manliness, Howard Dean's superdelegates, the ABC Stephanopoulos-Gibson debate) to Socrates' definitional refutations of Euthyphro and the Athenian elite. Like Socrates in Plato's cave allegory, Colbert is a shadow on the wall undermining truthiness from within, yet both fail: audiences laugh, guests collect the campaign-donation 'Colbert Bump,' and nothing changes, making America the self-satisfied one who is ignorant of its ignorance. Through Nehamas's contrast of Socratic and Platonic irony and the Symposium's demand that the greatest work read as both tragedy and comedy, the chapter concludes Colbert may be America's Plato — condemning and laughing at us like a Sisyphean liberator who knows we will not leave the cave.
- ch. 21 "Avowal, not an Owl" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein — Language Games — Stone builds a theory of humor from Wittgenstein's philosophy of language: Colbert's Starbucks-withdrawal 'ThreatDown' skit, the peg-leg-pirate quip at the Constitution Center, and the flip from '68% disapprove of the job he's doing' to '68% approve of the job he's not doing' all work as aspect-change (seeing-as), making us see an ordinary scene under a new aspect. Getting the joke requires a shared form of life (recognizing the Starbucks logo, knowing the Danish-cartoon controversy that made Colbert's suspiciously flattering entry on Islam the punchline) plus a personal Humorous Attitude and an avowal — laughter, or the Washington press corps' respectful silence at the 2006 Correspondents' Dinner, which Colbert converted into a second aspect-change for the larger TV and blog audience.
- ch. 22 "Moving On" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Alasdair MacIntyre — Authenticity — Frazier reads the show through Freud: Stephen play-acts both the repressed religious-right superego (Dobson, Hagee, his terror of bug sex) and the aggressive American id, so his improvised irony — shielding his crotch from Michael Stipe, mangling Teddy Roosevelt's big-stick maxim for Joe Sestak, sneering at the women's-softball sportsmanship story — works as therapeutic catharsis that lets viewers laugh at and tame their own aggression and hang-ups. Against MacIntyre's charge that irony corrodes culture, he enlists Kierkegaard's picture of the ironist who outdoes a view's 'ludicrous enthusiasm' (the U.S.A.! chant at Naomi Wolf, the gun-control interview that collapses into a case against itself), concluding that the man who merely played the true patriot was the more authentic American.
- ch. 23 "What Mr. Colbert Has Taught Us (Besides Everything)" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Übermensch; Will to Power; Master and Slave Morality; Ressentiment — In full truthiness voice, Michaud explains Colbert's failed 2008 presidential run — the South Carolina Democratic Executive Council's 13-3 vote keeping him off the ballot — as exactly what Nietzsche predicted: the resentful weak, the 'sheep,' hold the super-man down by redefining meekness as strength. He walks through will-to-power as self-overcoming, the lambs-and-birds-of-prey parable from the Genealogy, and Christianity as slave morality, then 'corrects' Nietzsche by relocating slave morality in the liberal media rather than God, ending with Colbert as the man of the future who 'affirms life without resentment.'
- ch. 24 "FINAL SEGMENT - What Stephen Colbert Tells Us about Being America" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "Truthiness and the Denial of Responsibility" *(no index entry yet)* — Schiller finds a calculated tension in Stephen: he claims impossible literal colorblindness ('People tell me I'm white and I believe them') while staging a nationwide search for a new black friend whose only function is to license racially insensitive talk, as in the Rosa Parks 'Overrated' WØRD where he misreads Alan's cursing as agreement. Working through the N-word debate (Kennedy's Intentionalism, Asim's Eradicationism, Chris Rock's double standard) and Michael Eric Dyson on Hurricane Katrina, he argues Stephen claims the rights of linguistic license while shirking its responsibilities, and that truthiness is the same posture writ large — the 'rhetoric of complexity' by which politicians deny responsibility for the problems they refuse to understand.
- ch. 26 "I’m Done But The Editor Expects Some Sort of Fancy Conclusion" **·** Socrates, Plato, Adam Smith, Thomas Hobbes — The Invisible Hand; Justice in the Republic — Smith dissects Stephen's free-market worship — the market as a God requiring faith, 'the market has spoken' on global warming, supply-side economics, and the plan to run universities as businesses with credit-card-swiper desks and tuition priced by marketability. Against this he deploys Socrates in the Republic: a practice is defined by its aim, so a physician aiming at his own wealth is not practicing medicine badly but moneymaking, and by the same argument a corporatized university whose primary aim is shareholder profit is no longer higher education — privatization alters its nature and so destroys it, while Smith's invisible hand is exposed as the South Park gnomes' missing Step Two and wikiality as supply-side epistemology where facts are supplied by majority vote instead of known.
- ch. 27 "Who Watches the Watchers" **·** Jean Baudrillard, Peter Singer — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); Climate Ethics — Patton and Webb unpack Colbert's coinage 'freem' — freedom without the do — from the first episode's dedication to 'the heroes' who act patriotically by watching TV, through Bush's post-9/11 call to go shopping, the Wikipedia elephant vandalism, and the WristStrong bracelet as activism indistinguishable from consuming Viacom product. Using Singer's argument that social capital (roads, satellites, infrastructure) makes the 'it's your money' cry hollow, E.O. Wilson's four-Earths arithmetic on unsustainable consumption and greenwashed market 'solutions' to global warming, and Baudrillard's Consumer Society account of news packaged for consumption beside the ads, they ask whether the Colbert Nation's ironic participation resists corporate media or completes it, concluding freem converts even critique into one more purchase.
- ch. 28 "TAKE THE ISHIHARA RACE TEST" *(no index entry yet)* — A mock color-blindness test: readers check figures to see whether they, like Stephen, suffer 'Colbertian Race Blindness,' an affliction of whites that confuses racial equality with racial indifference. The race-blind view history through that impairment — Civil Rights supposedly proved blacks and whites have 'perfectly identical cultures,' and Dr. King's colorblind society becomes a nation where everyone is one color, white — a gag that dramatizes the book's chapter on race by taking Stephen's 'I don't see race' literally.

## Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different

- ch. 1 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*

- ch. 8 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — The editor's introduction ('hello.') recounts his own path from an Apple IIe through a PC interlude back to the iPod and iPhone, and frames Jobs's arc: a bold, brash entrepreneur of modest means who revolutionized computers, music, phones, and movies, yet was petulant, insensitive, and cruel, a 'barefoot billionaire hippy capitalist' shaped by Sixties counterculture and Eastern spirituality who set out to 'make a ding in the universe.' It presents the book as neither demonization nor hagiography but thoughtful, mostly philosophical examinations of Jobs's life, work, and cultural impact from many points of view.
- ch. 10 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Mahon reads Jobs's 'reality distortion field'—the phrase Apple engineer Bud Tribble borrowed from the illusion-casting Talosians of Star Trek's 'The Cage' and 'The Menagerie'—through the ethics of deception. He argues that unlike the Talosians' non-consensual illusions (trapping Captain Pike to breed slaves), Jobs mostly changed people's beliefs about what was possible rather than deceiving them, often believed his own claims (even about his cancer), and sometimes freed people from false beliefs as the 1984 'Big Brother' Macintosh ad dramatized, so the field that produced the 'insanely great' Stevenotes, the impossible Macintosh schedule, and Dilbert's Dogbert parody needed little moral justification—and made Jobs's revolutionized industries possible.
- ch. 12 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** Karl Marx, Plato, Thomas Hobbes, John Rawls — Alienation; Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Ethical Egoism — Biondi argues the 'counter-cultural capitalist' is no paradox: Jobs succeeded not as a Gordon Gekko-style greedy capitalist but through the creative individualism of the cognitive counter-culture—the garage techno-geeks—who pursued their own vision rather than the bottom line. She traces the greedy-capitalist stereotype to Glaucon's Ring-of-Gyges challenge in Plato's Republic (people act justly only from fear of punishment), Hobbes's restless desire for power after power, and Marx and Engels's picture of alienated wage slavery under capitalism, with Rawls as the toleration-only-if-redistributed alternative. Jobs's hippie exterior (drugs, fruitarianism, Zen) masked an entrepreneur who, in Rand's 'creative mind' mold, put a ding in the universe through products like the iPad instead of philanthropy.
- ch. 13 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean; Master and Slave Morality; Will to Power — Noel measures Jobs against the four cardinal virtues from Plato's Republic and finds him wanting: imprudent (NeXT, the Lisa), unjust (taking the GUI from Xerox PARC, 'more fun to be a pirate'), intemperate (cruel outbursts like the 'dogshit for icing' cake), with only a brash, mind-changing courage. Drawing on Aristotle's golden mean from the Nicomachean Ethics, Nietzsche's master-slave morality and his Will to Power line about the man who 'determines values' for millennia, and Joseph Campbell's hero's journey, he argues entrepreneurs are a breed apart whose real virtues are independence of mind, vision, and audacity—and that Jobs, the anti-social creator who would not fit in, changed the world precisely because the cardinal virtues were 'prison walls' to him.
- ch. 14 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** John Searle — The Chinese Room; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Munkittrick argues that because personhood cannot be defined (trait lists like 'long-term planning' are circular) and behavior cannot prove an inner mind—as Searle's Chinese Room thought experiment shows—people have always identified persons intuitively, and Pixar trained Millennials to do exactly that. He reads the Pixar canon in three stages: Toy Story's self-aware Buzz as nascent non-human personhood, the Human-as-Partner films (Ratatouille's Remy and Linguini, WALL-E and EVE, Monsters, Inc.'s Sully and Boo, Up's Carl and Dug) as mutual recognition of persons across species lines, and The Incredibles as showing that even enhanced 'super-humans' face otherization—so a generation primed by these films will accept AI, animals, and uplifted beings as bearers of rights.
- ch. 15 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** Virtue Ethics; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Hicks starts from young Jobs the 'little terror' expelled from third grade and asks whether he failed the school system or the system failed him, answering that America's entrepreneurs are produced by culture outside school—garage workshops, Heathkits, dirt-bike ramps, and parents who back initiative—rather than rows, rote learning, and standardized tests. He catalogues the entrepreneurial character traits Jobs displayed (informed creative judgment, ambition and integrity like the carpenter's hidden plywood, initiative calling Bill Hewlett at home, courage, perseverance through the Lisa, NeXT, and Pixar losses, win-win trade, leadership) and proposes risk-exercise curricula, Montessori methods, and programs like NFTE so schooling can deliberately cultivate the virtues of a flourishing entrepreneurial life.
- ch. 17 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** Adam Smith, Ralph Waldo Emerson — The Invisible Hand; Self-Reliance; Ethical Egoism — Salvino casts Jobs as a billionaire egoist-visionary in the lineage of Adam Smith's insight that an entrepreneur's self-interest, not good intentions, best satisfies people's wants, Emerson's self-reliance, and Rand's virtues of independence and integrity—comparing Jobs to Howard Roark while noting his intuition was 'un-Randianly' unreasoned. Through Schumpeterian creative destruction (the automobile killing the horse-and-carriage; Wozniak's Apple I that HP rejected) and Deming's quality-first management, he explains Jobs's 'faster horse' contempt for market research, then rebuts the three standard ethical complaints—Foxconn labor conditions, his harsh verbal lashings, and his refusal to join the Giving Pledge—arguing Jobs did more good making the iPad than philanthropy ever could.
- ch. 18 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Krause and Parker take on the charge that Jobs 'didn't invent anything'—Wozniak was the engineer, Xerox PARC had the GUI, MP3 players and smartphones already existed—by deploying Ayn Rand's objective theory of value, which rejects both intrinsic value in things and subjective value as whim. On Rand's distinction between 'philosophically objective' value (the best possible by the most rational mind, e.g. technically superior PCs) and 'socially objective' value (the sum of individual judgments in trade, her lipstick-versus-microscope example), Jobs's genius was converting the first into the second—making ease-of-use valuable to the early majority with the iMac, iPod, and iPhone—so inventing is neither necessary nor sufficient for entrepreneurship, and Jobs deserves the wealth and admiration his market success brought.
- ch. 19 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** David Hume, Philippa Foot — Reason Is the Slave of the Passions; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Thomas asks whether the Apple II, Macintosh, and iPod were great products regardless of sales or great because they sold, and answers that market success is real evidence of value: each sale is a buyer's revealed preference in a voluntary trade, a stronger test than critics or focus groups, which is why Jobs's flops (NeXT, the G4 Cube) were overdesigned, overpriced failures of utility rather than quality. Against Hume's quoted doctrine that reason is and ought only to be the slave of the passions (hunger strikers and Jobs's own vegan fanaticism defeat any basic-desire theory), he follows Rand and Philippa Foot in grounding value in objective human needs and capacities, so products designed for those needs—like the iPhone the Apple team built for themselves—could be expected to succeed.
- ch. 20 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 21 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** Peter Singer, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill, Aristotle, Jeremy Bentham — The Drowning Child (obligation to aid); Humanity as an End in Itself; The Categorical Imperative; The Harm Principle — Framed by Dickens's Jacob Marley, Walker asks whether Jobs deserved his posthumous accolades despite giving far less to charity than Bill Gates, and tests him under three frameworks. Aristotle's virtue ethics acquits him (character is judged holistically, and charity sits near the golden mean of open-handedness rather than being a checklisted duty); Mill's utilitarianism acquits him (his innovations maximized happiness and he violated no Harm Principle—though abandoning daughter Lisa counts as a harm); and Singer's drowning-child argument condemns him as near-morally-bankrupt for selling luxury gadgets while children starve. Kant both convicts (charity is an imperfect duty under the categorical imperative) and saves Jobs: treating the affluent individual as an end in himself, never merely a means to the destitute, blocks Singer's demand for giving to marginal utility.
- ch. 22 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** The Buddha, David Hume — The Four Noble Truths; Non-Self (anatman); Zen Buddhism; Bundle Theory of Self — Klein and Fundora trace Jobs's Buddhism from Reed College meditation and the seven-month India pilgrimage (reading Yogananda's Autobiography of a Yogi yearly) to the Zen minimalism of Apple design, arguing his temper tantrums, harsh speech, and reality distortion field do not disqualify him from being 'on the path' since Buddhism is a practice, not a creed test. They expound the Four Noble Truths (dukkha in its three kinds, via Thich Nhat Hanh), the Eightfold Path's Middle Way, and anatta—the non-self they compare to Hume's bundle theory of the self against Descartes's thinking thing—and read Jobs's strip-away-the-essence aesthetics, the three-click intuitive iPod interface that keeps users in the moment, the non-dualist marriage of art and technology, and his Think Different self-reliance as deeply Buddhist authenticity.
- ch. 23 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** The Problem of Evil — White argues Apple's 'Think Different' commercial packages together two distinct character traits: genuine independence, in Rand's sense of judging from the facts of reality (thirteen-year-old Jobs confronting his pastor with the problem of evil via the Biafran children—'Does God know about this?'—rejecting dogma at Stanford, killing the iPod's screen, bending Corning to make gorilla glass on schedule), and pseudo-independence that asserts the primacy of consciousness over reality (refusing to bathe because his diet 'prevented' odor, treating cancer with fruit juice, NeXT's impossible eighteen-month promise). Using Binswanger's 'fallacy of false integration' (the surgeon-and-murderer 'cutter' example), he charges the ad with merging the traits into one folder, so Jobs should instead be praised without qualification for his independence and blamed without qualification for his pseudo-independence.
- ch. 24 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Practical Wisdom (phronesis); The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics — Meyer reads Jobs through 'individualistic perfectionism'—the Aristotelian tradition (via Rasmussen and Den Uyl, and Veatch) on which flourishing is objective to human nature yet agent-relative, an endless striving unique to each person's talents rather than Kant's by-the-book categorical imperative applied impersonally to all. Jobs embodied this: the 'bicycle of the mind' faith that reason and tools extend human efficiency, practical wisdom weighing goods like friendship, health, and art through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, experimental self-discovery (Zen, calligraphy, fruitarian diets), and the exile-to-NeXT-to-Pixar-to-iMac arc of constant re-evaluation—so the right question is not whether Jobs 'was' a moral perfectionist but whether each of us keeps striving in our own key.
- ch. 25 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** Intentionality; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Iuliano asks whether it even makes sense to blame Apple (not Tim Cook or the board) for the Foxconn suicides, child labor, pollution, or tax evasion, laying out the two conditions of moral agency—autonomy and the capacity to know right from wrong—via the blameless wasp. He then canvasses the corporate moral agency debate: Peter French's Corporate Internal Decision structures, which filter employees' personal reasons into corporate ones (the dividend example), and List and Pettit's functionalist group agency, whose judgment-aggregation paradox (three executives, an environmentally friendly but harmful factory) shows Apple's moral conclusions can diverge from every member's—against Quinton's 'sum of its parts' reduction—so holding the corporation itself responsible plugs the responsibility deficit left when no individual is blameworthy.
- ch. 26 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Søren Kierkegaard, William James — Bad Faith; Authenticity; Despair (sickness unto death); The Pragmatic Method — Pardi argues Jobs lived philosophically as an existentialist: the 'Steve Jobs Roll Your Own Calculator Construction Set' anecdote shows design by touch and intuition rather than master plans, every detail of a product mattered because it belongs to a life narrative of 'making a ding in the universe,' and he avoided both Kierkegaard's despair (the gap between actual and possible self) and Sartrean bad faith—quoted from Being and Nothingness—by never lying to himself about his products, calling faulty work 'shit' and redoing it. Against him stands Bill Gates the pragmatist, whose utilitarian Windows-for-every-desk business and 'rationality only goes so far' humility embody William James's pragmatic method, while Jobs's Zune taunt ('we made the iPod for ourselves') shows the existentialist refusing to compromise authenticity for market share.
- ch. 28 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** Ethical Egoism; Utilitarianism — Cohen retells the DOJ ebook case—Amazon's $9.99 Kindle pricing, Eddy Cue's agency-model deals with the five publishers, the most-favored-nation clause, Jobs's warning email to James Murdoch, and Judge Cote's conspiracy ruling—to ask whether Jobs and other businessmen live and work to serve consumers or themselves. He argues antitrust law encodes the altruist-utilitarian demand that producers sacrifice their own goals to consumer welfare, and defends the Randian alternative ('your life belongs to you') on which Jobs, Cue, and the publishers were entitled to pursue their own happiness through their work, so readers inspired by Jobs's 'find what you love' Stanford challenge should reject the ethics behind antitrust.
- ch. 29 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** Martin Heidegger, Aristotle — The Question Concerning Technology; The Four Causes — In an imagined Walter Cronkite-moderated afterlife debate, Jobs opens with 'most technology is shit,' holding up the iPod as art-through-simplicity—design as the soul of the thing, thought down to its essence—while Heidegger answers from 'The Question Concerning Technology': the iPod's four Aristotelian causes (material, form, purpose, maker) work together as co-responsible bringing-forth, a revealing whose essence is enframing, which conceals the human when technology is treated as mere standing-reserve and cheapest utility. The dialogue converges on Jobs's washer-and-dryer anecdote and the Mercedes line: technology that reveals rather than conceals our being—useful and beautiful—keeps it serving humanity instead of mastering it, and Heidegger's Nazi past is flagged for the reader to judge separately.
- ch. 30 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Immanuel Kant — The Dialectic; Phenomena and Noumena; Transcendental Idealism — Knepp asks why Jobs's 'simplicity is the ultimate sophistication' produced the friendly, MoMA-collected Macintosh (the face-like design, the inviting handle, the signed internals) but collapsed into the $6,500 NeXT Cube, answering with Žižek's reading of Hegel in Less than Nothing: the original idea is already self-contradictory, the failure of NeXT (the over-engineered perfect cube, the $100,000 Rand logo trying too hard to be friendly) is its symptom, and the iMac is the second attempt that only the failed first choice makes possible. He grounds this in Kant's Critique of Pure Reason—the antinomies and the phenomenon/noumenon distinction that Hegel radicalized into a world driven by oppositions—finding the dialectic everywhere in Jobs: two sets of parents, orchards and Silicon Valley, 'Apple' as both high-tech and organic, and a childish lowercase signature made with grand cursive flair.
- ch. 31 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Stranger Things and Philosophy Thus Spake the Demogorgon" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Stranger Things and Philosophy Thus Spake the Demogorgon" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Thanks" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "How to Make Something Strange Even Stranger" **·** Authenticity — Andrew Winters's introduction argues the show appeals both to those who lived the Eighties and those who wish they had: plastic, story-rich 1980s childhoods (D&D, bikes, walkie-talkies) versus a present of single-bit tweets, likes, and Instagram-filtered self-display where we look to others for confirmation instead of creating worlds together. It then previews the volume's essays on horror's appeal, whether monsters like Dart are all evil, friendship and civil disobedience, the Shadow Monster within ourselves, Will's possession and identity, nostalgia and forgetting, and Eleven's faith and heroism as a guide to meaningful living, closing with Hopper's 'Mornings are for coffee and contemplation.'
- ch. 10 "I Strange Thoughts" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "1. Barb Dead, People Mad" **·** Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Holmes and Christensen read the #JusticeForBarb movement through Baudrillard's hyperreality: fans mobilized real activism for a fictional girl the show killed as a plot device (dragged by the Demogorgon while Nancy and Steve are upstairs), while real murdered women like Jamie Haggard got no hashtag, so fictional justice becomes 'more real than the real.' The show itself is a simulacrum assembled from 1980s movies (E.T., Poltergeist, Firestarter, The Goonies, Stand by Me) whose grid motif casts the series as a D&D gameboard the audience plays, and the chapter argues hyperreal power became real power when the Duffers gave Barb a Season Two funeral and apology from Hawkins Lab.
- ch. 12 "2. Can Anything Good Come from the Upside Down" **·** Augustine of Hippo — The Two Cities; The Problem of Evil — Kuzma maps Augustine's two cities onto the two Hawkinses: not two places but two mixed moral orientations in one world, since Will is literally 'right here' in the same house flipped upside down. Augustine's privation view of evil (evil as absence of good, a nougat-less Three Musketeers) explains how Dart can come from the 'evil' Upside Down yet love Dustin and let the party pass, while Brenner, from the right side up, is ruled by libido dominandi like the Mind Flayer and Dr. Owens proves Hawkins Lab is not automatically bad; it is how you act, not where you are from.
- ch. 13 "3. Save the Demogorgons!" **·** Peter Singer, Jeremy Bentham, Tom Regan — Speciesism; Animal Liberation; Animal Rights (subjects-of-a-life); Anthropocentrism — Puumala asks whether killing the Demogorgons is speciesist: Dart's pain response to light makes the demodogs sentient (Bentham's 'Can they suffer?'), giving them moral considerability, while the Mind Flayer may or may not be a moral agent and could even be a keystone species whose destruction collapses the Upside Down ecosystem. He tests whether demogorgons count as invasive species (they may be native to a causally connected mirror dimension), invokes Regan's lifeboat case to argue they must still lose out to humans in a conflict of interests, and ends with the uncomfortable thought that humans are themselves an invasive species turning Earth into an Upside Down, so Eleven closing the gate was compassionate conservation.
- ch. 14 "II The Joy of the Creepy" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "4. The Slimy, Macabre, and Horrific in Stranger Things" **·** Plato — Nisley applies Noel Carroll's account of art-horror to the Demogorgon: categorically transgressive, interdimensional monsters provoke thought-based fear and disgust (the shed goop, the hazmat suits, Barb's blood in the pool), and it is precisely this disgust that makes our curiosity about the monster's origin and disclosure pleasurable. She traces Nancy's investigation from Jonathan's photograph to the bear trap, brings in Plato's Leontius story from the Republic and Kieran and Feagin on the grotesque to explain why we paradoxically delight in Barb's slime-covered corpse and Will coughing up a slug, and concludes that revulsion amplifies the fascination that keeps us watching.
- ch. 16 "5. Horror Appeals to Our Dual Nature" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — Despair (sickness unto death); Anxiety (the dizziness of freedom) — Allaire and Gehring argue horror works on Kierkegaard's dual nature, the tug-of-war between finitude and infinitude that produces despair: the show's corporeal terrors (the Demogorgon's kills, Barb's decomposing body with a slug in its mouth, Will's tentacle) trigger the fear of mutilation and extinction, while the intelligent Shadow Monster shatters our sense of being unique, echoing Ernest Becker's claim that we build cultural 'armor' against mortality. Using Carroll's paradox of horror and Stephen King's three levels (revulsion, horror, terror), they contend we enjoy confronting these fears safely from the couch, with the Shadow Monster looming over the Snow Ball as an emblem of real horrors, from AIDS to 9/11, still to come.
- ch. 17 "6. The Unique Horror of the Upside Down" **·** Martin Heidegger — Dasein (being-there); The They-Self (das Man) — Pamerleau argues the Upside Down's distinctive horror is not its monsters, which offer familiar Jaws-style jump scares and supervillain plots, but the place itself: reading Will through Heidegger's Dasein and being-in-the-world, our selves are constituted by the web of socially inherited meanings (the 'they') attached to familiar places and things. Waking in a dead replica of home, where the same houses, school, and Castle Byers no longer function or answer back, forces Will to spell 'R-I-G-H-T H-E-R-E' through the lights, an uncanny juxtaposition of the familiar and the alien that the chapter compares to an open-casket funeral and contrasts with Alien's wholly unknown ship.
- ch. 18 "III Nothing Is Stranger than Reality" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "7. The Mind Flayer through a Gnostic Lens" **·** Plato, Plotinus — Theory of Forms; Neoplatonism (the One) — Ewing reads the Mind Flayer as the Demiurge of the Upside Down, a dark derivative copy of our world complete with replicated Castle Byers and school decorations: he surveys Plato's Timaeus craftsman who shapes chaotic matter on the model of the Forms, Plotinus's One and its secondary demiurge, and the Gnostic variants, from the Valentinian just-but-imperfect craftsman to the Sethian Yaldabaoth, a serpent-faced false god who steals divine power. Because the Mind Flayer hive-minds Will and the demodogs, wants to conquer our dimension as a 'master race,' and hates the real world rather than serving it, the chapter concludes it matches the Sethian evil Demiurge, an incorporeal entity playing at being god.
- ch. 20 "8. In Eggos We Trust" **·** Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Wigley uses Baudrillard's hyperreality and semiotics to argue that Eggos, not Eleven, are Hawkins's true savior: as Barb's Xeroxed missing-poster face drifts through generations of models away from the original photo, so Eggos accumulate new symbolic value as tokens of trust and friendship, from Mike's blanket-fort promise of 'as many Eggos as you want' to Hopper's box in the snow-covered woods that tells El she can come home. The Party's Dungeons & Dragons vocabulary (naming the Demogorgon, Dustin's 'best metaphor') is their shared code for making sense of a reality shattered by adolescence, Reagan-era image politics, and the Upside Down, and the trust the waffles symbolize extends past the screen to the viewer.
- ch. 21 "9. To Err Is Human, to Forget … Sublime" **·** John Locke — Personal Identity (memory theory); Personal Identity — Huntingford contrasts Stranger Things with its blueprint, Stephen King's It: where It forces the Losers Club back to the traumatic truth of childhood, the show traffics in 'false nostalgia,' vicarious nostalgia for an Eighties that only existed on screen, supported by Loftus's false-memory experiments (the impossible Bugs Bunny, Stewart's Root Beer) and Will's anniversary effect and El's mother's broken record of 'breathe, sunflower, rainbow... 450.' Against this malleability she sets Locke's memory theory of personal identity from the Essay and Sacks's 'lost mariner,' warning that nostalgic self-deception can rewrite the self, yet concluding, with It's own ending, that since we cannot survive some horrors, the comforting lie of misremembered childhood is what we tune in for.
- ch. 22 "IV How Strange Are We" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "10. Stranger Shadows" **·** Carl Jung — The Shadow; Archetypes; The Collective Unconscious — Cornell reads the Upside Down as an externalized Jungian Shadow: the faceless Demogorgon, 'almost human but it wasn't,' embodies the archetypal shadow of the collective unconscious intruding into Hawkins, and the moral task is integrating it with the conscious ego. Will's possession by the Shadow Monster shows what Jung calls the ego identifying with an unintegrated shadow (his timidity leaving him overpowered), while El is the contrast: after her symbolic rebirth from the fleshy wall she faces absolute evil, acknowledges her own monstrous capacity to kill, and turns the shadow into heroism, ending at Nietzsche's 'becoming who she is.'
- ch. 24 "11. Not from Around Here" **·** Michel Foucault — Power/Knowledge — Zanin applies Foucault's Abnormal lectures, where a monster is a juridico-natural being violating both the laws of nature and of society, to the show: the Demogorgon and demodogs break biology and morality, while El and Eight are biologically abnormal (psionic) and law-breaking, making them Foucauldian monsters too, as Lucas's 'maybe she's the monster?' suggests. Monsters emerge wherever power/knowledge assemblages operate, hence Hawkins Lab's MK-Ultra-style experimentation conjuring the very Demogorgon it hunts, and the chapter extends monstrosity to human 'assholes' like Brenner, Lonnie, and Billy before concluding that knowing the monster, being a freak, is a virtue and a weapon against fear.
- ch. 25 "12. Who Is Will Byers" **·** Personal Identity — Hammonds and Gordon use Mead's symbolic interactionism, in which the self emerges from interaction and stabilizes around 'identity anchors' others can expect, to unpack 'Zombie Boy': Mr. Clarke's Phineas Gage story frames Max's doubt that Will is still Will, Joyce's hovering and Will's fragile-child role co-constitute each other, and Will renegotiates a different identity with Jonathan ('Stop treating me like I'm gonna break'). During the Mind Flayer's possession, when Will screams that the creature is 'everywhere,' his family's stories of the toy truck and the crayon spaceship summon the kind, honest anchors of the old Will, showing identity as recognizable and stable yet ultimately negotiable, and that realizing and actualizing agency lets Will beat the role the monster assigned him.
- ch. 26 "V How Do We Cope with the Strange" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "13. Kids on Civil Disobedience" **·** Henry David Thoreau — Civil Disobedience — Guerra and Barkman argue the Party and Hopper practice Thoreauvian civil disobedience: the boys sneak out at night despite Hopper's explicit order, Hopper breaks into Hawkins Lab twice and exposes the fake body in the quarry, and the kids steal Billy's car to reach Will because 'a Party member requires assistance.' They accept Thoreau's point that disobeying unjust laws is right even at great risk, then distill three tests from the show for when laws should be broken: laws made with bad intent (the Lab's secrecy and human experimentation), laws contradicted by new knowledge (anything ignoring the Upside Down), and laws that block a greater good (speeding to save a dying stranger, trespassing to save Will).
- ch. 28 "14. Friends Don’t Lie" **·** Aristotle, Friedrich Nietzsche, Carol Gilligan, Nel Noddings, Jacques Derrida — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); The Ethics of Care; Virtue Ethics — Bowman tests Hawkins friendships against Aristotle's three kinds in the Nicomachean Ethics: Dustin and Lucas's shared-comics pleasure collapses into rivalry over Max, Nancy and Jonathan's utility ends once Will and Barb are found, and Barb's fatal poolside loyalty to Nancy, though one-directional, is a friendship of virtue. Nietzsche's ideal of friends who strengthen us through conflict recasts those very fights (Lucas confronting Eleven's power misuse) as the best friendship, care ethics (Gilligan and Noddings) makes the mutual one-caring Party the real answer to who teaches Eleven friendship, and Derrida's Politics of Friendship grounds democracy and society itself in such everyday reciprocity, which is why Eleven's 'friends don't lie' compass pulls her back from Kali's violence to close the gate.
- ch. 29 "15. Abnormal Is the New Normal" **·** Michel Foucault — Power/Knowledge; Discipline and Docile Bodies — Berns, Foronda, and Zarate read the show anachronistically (via Didi-Huberman), arguing its millennial sensibilities deliberately clash with the 1980s setting to reveal that normalcy is a shifting social discourse rather than a natural fact: Joyce defends Will's possible sexuality like no 1980s mother would, Jonathan claims freakishness as a right, and audiences mourn plain, awkward Barb. Through Foucault's three figures from Abnormal, the monster (androgynous, tomboy-coded Eleven called 'freak'), the individual to be corrected (hippie Terry Ives, 'hysterical' Joyce, un-macho boys), and the masturbator (surveillance of the most intimate life), plus biopolitics and bullying as State-sanctioned discipline, they show the abnormal are the heroes: 'The X-Men are weirdos.'
- ch. 30 "16. Gotta Have Faith" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, David Hume — Teleological Suspension of the Ethical; Faith and Reason; Problem of Induction — Winters asks what faith is when the Party risks burning and becoming demodog chow so Eleven can close the gate: after arguing via George Michael and the talisman-free tunnels that faith need not be religious, he tests Bishop's models of faith against 'The Gate' (the affective and secular hope models fit; the belief and trust models fail because everyone has seen the Mind Flayer's work on Will). Hume's account that causation is never observed, only habituated, explains the Party's hope that heat will drive the Mind Flayer from Will and that Christmas lights will reach him, and Kierkegaard's teleological suspension of the ethical and knight of faith frame Eleven's willingness to die against the absurd, since aligning her life with friendship's higher purpose is what makes it meaningful.
- ch. 31 "Bibliography" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "The Party" *(notes)*
- ch. 33 "Index" *(notes)*

## Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Superheroes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Men in Bright Tights and Wild Fights, Often at Great Heights, and, of Course," *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction surveys the current resurgence of the superhero: Spider-Man's record-breaking opening weekends, 87,000 fans at the San Diego Comicon, and superhero references running through Seinfeld, Scrubs, rock, and rap. It argues that classic superhero stories, like the works of Plato and Aristotle, are here to stay - enduring modern myths that are wildly fun yet thought-provoking, with Superman and Batman now recognized worldwide as cultural icons.
- ch. 6 "Superheroes and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors argue that superhero comics, an original American art form like jazz, deserve serious intellectual attention because they dramatize philosophy's deepest questions - ethics, responsibility, justice, personal identity, faith, friendship, and family. They press the point into the near future: genetic engineering and nanotechnology may soon make real the questions comics have long explored, such as whether to genetically supercharge a baby or what to do if you woke up with powers yourself. The volume brings philosophy professors together with comic-book writers and editors to wrestle with these issues.
- ch. 7 "Superheroes and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 8 "Part One - The Image of the Superhero" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Chapter 1 - The Real Truth about Superman And the Rest of Us, Too" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "Preparation for a Surprise" *(interlude)*
- ch. 11 "The One Question I Could Not Answer" **·** Socrates — Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — Comic writer Mark Waid, hired by DC editor Dan DiDio to re-imagine Superman in Superman: Birthright, is stumped by the question 'Why does he do what he does?' He argues that post-9/11 kids see the Big Blue Boy Scout as an ultraconservative protector of a corrupt status quo, making him irrelevant to a generation that knows heroes from metal detectors and assassinated visionaries. Invoking Socrates' claim that the genuine search for wisdom begins with admitting we do not know, Waid resolves to unlearn a lifetime of Superman lore, and locates the key to the character's motivation in Kal-El's utter aloneness: he is the sole survivor of Krypton and 'doesn't belong here'.
- ch. 12 "The Need to Belong" **·** Aristotle — Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Working out Birthright's answer, Waid argues that even the solar-powered Kal-El shares the human need to belong, so he can connect with humanity not by hiding his alien side but by embracing it. Echoing a Marianne Williamson passage about our fear of being 'powerful beyond measure', Waid has Superman wear the S-shield - the banner of his Kryptonian 'tribe' - and use his powers openly, because only by living authentically in service of others does he truly belong. He links this to Aristotle's discovery that happiness is rooted in living with excellence, which Superman 'in his own way' found too.
- ch. 13 "The Great Paradox" **·** Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Waid closes by drawing out the paradox that Superman's shining selflessness is achieved through acting in his own self-interest: in saving others he exercises his distinctive powers and fulfills his authentic destiny, which fulfills him, while embracing his own nature and history puts him in the one activity that most helps others. There is no blanket choice between self and community, he argues - properly fulfilling one's own nature redounds to everyone's benefit - and Superman thereby becomes a mirror for examining the balance of selflessness and self-interest in the reader's own life.
- ch. 14 "Chapter 2 - Heroes and Superheroes" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "Defining a Hero and a Superhero" **·** Virtue Ethics — Loeb and Morris take on the argument that 'superhero' is an oxymoron - the more super (and invulnerable) a being, the less it risks, so the less heroic it can be, which would disqualify Superman except under Kryptonite. They rebut it by insisting heroism is a moral category: a hero is a person of noble character whose worthy achievements are guided by the good, so a superhero is a person of noble character with superhuman powers or superhumanly developed abilities, which gets Batman and Green Arrow into the fray. They extend heroism to everyday firefighters, nurses, and stay-at-home mothers, and use J. Jonah Jameson's resentment of Spider-Man to show how the hero's sacrifice stands as a standing rebuke to spectators' inertia.
- ch. 16 "How to Be a Hero" **·** Plato — Virtue Ethics — Using Superman for All Seasons, the authors argue that Clark's heroic choice required real sacrifice - leaving his family, Smallville, and Lana Lang to serve more people - and that sacrifice and the self-discipline behind it are underappreciated virtues, down payments on great goods attainable no other way, as with Peter Parker and Matt Murdock too. The hero, they say, is a normative concept with a claim on us, and since Plato held that the good is inherently attractive and draws us toward it, well-told superhero stories have genuine moral force, keeping self-discipline, self-sacrifice, and aspiration alive while entertaining us.
- ch. 17 "Fear and the Superhero Stories" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — The authors argue superhero stories speak to our fears twice: first by dramatizing external dangers (mad scientists, terrorists, alien menaces), and second by confronting the subtler fear of what using violence will do to our own souls, since habit and a 'rising threshold' of expectations can make once-unthinkable force come to seem necessary. Superheroes like Batman, Spider-Man, Daredevil, and Superman model the answer: they exercise force within strict limits and draw lines they will not cross, fighting evil without becoming evil, and so show that courage, determination, and character can prevail against adversity.
- ch. 18 "The Example of the Superhero" **·** Seneca — Virtue Ethics — Quoting Seneca's advice to 'choose for yourself a moral hero' as an ethical pattern and to 'live as if he were watching you', the chapter argues that superheroes can function for us exactly as the Stoic recommended: Superman inspires us, Batman keeps us going when the going is tough, Spider-Man teaches that conscience outranks the crowd's voices, and Daredevil shows that limitations need not hold us back. It closes practically: ask 'What would Superman do?' and go do your version of it.
- ch. 19 "Chapter 3 - The Crimson Viper versus the Maniacal Morphing Meme" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "What the Problem Seems to Be" *(interlude)*
- ch. 21 "What the Problem Is" **·** Heraclitus — Everything Flows / Logos — In dialogue form, Dennis O'Neil diagnoses the fan's complaint that 'the new Viper sucks' as an attempt to do what Heraclitus said cannot be done - step into the same river twice. He reinforces the point with the I Ching's teaching that things become their opposites (yin into yang, light into darkness) and with Darwin's evolution, arguing that constant change is simply the nature of things, comic-book characters included.
- ch. 22 "The One Constant Is Change" **·** Heraclitus — Everything Flows / Logos — O'Neil develops two lenses on why the thirty-year-old Crimson Viper cannot stay the same, the first being Jungian archetypes: superheroes are modern incarnations of ancient figures - Superman is, in Jerry Siegel's own words, 'Samson, Hercules, and all the strong men I ever heard of rolled into one - only more so', the Flash a Mercury, Wonder Woman an Amazon, Thor lifted from Norse myth. Myths always mutated as bards adjusted tales to audience feedback around the campfire (Homer included), and modern media markets merely deliver that feedback faster through sales, ratings, and instant web response, so creators reshape characters quickly.
- ch. 23 "The Scheme of the Meme" **·** Everything Flows / Logos — Defining the meme via the OED and Richard Dawkins - a cultural element spread by imitation that mutates like a gene under selection - O'Neil explains why heroes transform: creators get new ideas, markets demand new stories, authors age, new writers arrive, popularity wanes, or an executive has a brainstorm. The evidence ranges over Superman escalating from leaping tall buildings to near-light speed, Batman morphing from 1930s gentleman crime-fighter to Adam West comedian to dark avenger, radio adding Jimmy Olsen and Kryptonite, the Hulk changing color, and Green Lantern changing identity from Alan Scott to Hal Jordan to Kyle Rayner. Gradual change feels organic; the returning fan simply finds the evolved meme unrecognizable.
- ch. 24 "What We Want and What We Get" **·** Heraclitus — Everything Flows / Logos — O'Neil concludes that fans want writers to 'preserve a part of their childhood', an impossible wish since new stories must change the meme-archetype and somebody will always be outraged. He adds a second Heraclitean twist: the reader has changed too, so you cannot step into the same river twice for two reasons - the Viper is no longer your Viper, and you are no longer his reader. The essay ends with a cosmic flourish about the Viper joining 'the vast, timeless dance of Being', met by the fan's deflating 'Still sucks.'
- ch. 25 "Chapter 4 - Superhero Revisionism in Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns" *(front)*
